sections.title: Market balance
sections.question: What is the current Pakistan fertilizer supply-demand balance, how have production, imports, offtake and inventory changed, and what does the evidence imply about near-term tightness or oversupply?
sections.answer:
## Direct answer

Pakistan's fertilizer market entered Kharif 2026 with a **comfortable urea surplus but a structurally tight DAP position**. As of April 2026, urea closing inventory was 805 thousand tonnes against monthly offtake of 463 thousand tonnes—roughly 1.7 months of cover. DAP closing inventory was 203 thousand tonnes against monthly offtake of 85 thousand tonnes—about 2.4 months of cover, but projected to fall to just 17 thousand tonnes by September 2026. The near-term outlook is **urea oversupply with price stability risk, and DAP tightness requiring uninterrupted gas supply and timely imports**.

## What changed

- **Urea offtake surged**: April 2026 offtake was 463 thousand tonnes, up 84.9% year-on-year (from 251 thousand tonnes in April 2025) [P001][P003].
- **DAP offtake declined**: 85 thousand tonnes, down 10.8% year-on-year, attributed to higher prices [P001][P003].
- **Total nutrient offtake rose 44.1%** year-on-year to 320 thousand tonnes; nitrogen up 62%, potash up 55.1%, phosphate down 5% [P001][P003].
- **Production was stable**: Total domestic production in April 2026 was 709 thousand tonnes; urea 476 thousand tonnes, DAP 74 thousand tonnes [P001][P003].
- **Imports were minimal**: Only 5.1 thousand tonnes total (AS, SOP, MOP, TSP); zero urea and zero DAP imports in April 2026 [P003][P013].
- **Inventory position**: Urea closing balance rose marginally from 804 to 805 thousand tonnes; DAP fell from 214 to 203 thousand tonnes [P004][P005].
- **Kharif 2026 projections were revised upward** between the March and April reviews: urea availability raised from 3,847 to 4,083 thousand tonnes; closing stock raised from 483 to 574 thousand tonnes. DAP availability raised from 655 to 711 thousand tonnes (adding 55 thousand tonnes of imports), but closing stock still projected at only 17 thousand tonnes [P005][P017].
- **Prices rose across the board** in April 2026 versus March: urea (sona) +1.8%, DAP +2.9%, SSP +3.8%, SOP +6% [P001].

## Decisive evidence

| Claim | Evidence | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Urea offtake 463 kt in April 2026, +84.9% y/y | "Urea offtake was 463 thousand tonnes which increased by 84.9 per cent" | [P001] |
| DAP offtake 85 kt, -10.8% y/y | "DAP offtake was 85 thousand tonnes which decreased by 10.8 per cent" | [P001][P003] |
| Total nutrient offtake 320 kt, +44.1% y/y | "Total nutrient offtake during April 2026 was 320 thousand tonnes, which increased by 44.1 per cent" | [P001][P003] |
| Urea production 476 kt; DAP 74 kt in April 2026 | "Urea and DAP production was 476 and 74 thousand tonnes, respectively" | [P001][P003] |
| Total production 709 kt in April 2026 | "Total domestic fertilizer production during April 2026 was 709 thousand tonnes" | [P001][P003] |
| Imports negligible: 5.1 kt total; zero urea/DAP | "Imported supplies comprised of 3 thousand tonnes of AS, 0.1 thousand tonne of SOP, 1.1 thousand tonne of MOP and one thousand tonne of TSP" | [P003] |
| Urea closing inventory 805 kt; DAP 203 kt | "leaving a closing balance of 805 thousand tonnes" (urea); "leaving closing balance of 203 thousand tonnes" (DAP) | [P004] |
| Kharif 2026 urea: availability 4,083 kt; demand 3,498 kt; closing 574 kt | "Total availability of urea is estimated at 4,083 thousand tonnes...Urea demand during Kharif 2026 is projected around 3,498 thousand tonnes, showing 574 thousand tonnes of closing stock" | [P002][P005] |
| Kharif 2026 DAP: availability 711 kt; demand 695 kt; closing 17 kt | "expected availability of DAP during Kharif 2026 is around 711 thousand tonnes...DAP demand is estimated around 695 thousand tonnes" | [P002][P005] |
| DAP imports of 55 kt scheduled Jun-Jul 2026 | "Imported supplies: 0, 0, 35, 20, 0, 0" (Jun, Jul) | [P005] |
| All domestic prices rose in April 2026 | "Prices of all fertilizer products increased during month under review compared with March 2026" | [P001] |
| FY2025-26 (Jul-Apr) urea offtake 5,880 kt, +21.6% vs prior year | Annex-4: urea total 7,163,885 (annualized); Apr cumulative 5,880,208 | [P009][P015] |
| FY2025-26 (Jul-Apr) DAP offtake 1,260 kt, -4.2% vs prior year | Annex-4: DAP total 1,476,957 (annualized); Apr cumulative 1,260,295 | [P009][P015] |

## Interpretation

**Urea is in surplus.** The Kharif 2026 projection shows availability of 4,083 thousand tonnes against demand of 3,498 thousand tonnes, leaving 574 thousand tonnes of closing stock—an excess of 274 thousand tonnes over projected demand [P005]. The April 2026 actuals confirm this: production (476 kt) exceeded offtake (463 kt), and inventory was essentially flat at 805 kt [P004]. The NFDC's caution that "operation of all the urea manufacturing plants at full capacity during Kharif is crucial for smooth supply and price stability" [P002] signals that the risk is not shortage but potential oversupply pressure on prices, particularly given the sharp year-on-year offtake recovery (+84.9% in April) that may not be sustained.

**DAP is tight and deteriorating.** The Kharif projection shows availability of 711 thousand tonnes against demand of 695 thousand tonnes, leaving only 17 thousand tonnes of closing stock—essentially zero buffer [P005]. This projection depends on: (a) 55 thousand tonnes of imports arriving in June-July [P005]; (b) uninterrupted gas supply to the local DAP plant [P002]; and (c) offtake following the five-year average. The March 2026 review projected a **negative** closing stock of -31 thousand tonnes for DAP [P017], which was only corrected by adding 55 thousand tonnes of imports in the April review [P005]. This indicates the balance is fragile and import-dependent.

**Demand recovery is underway but uneven.** FY2025-26 (Jul-Apr) urea offtake is running 21.6% above the prior year, while DAP is down 4.2% [P009]. The annual review attributed the prior year's decline to "poor farm economics due to low market prices of wheat" and projected an 8.7% nutrient demand recovery in 2025-26 [P020][P022]. The April data is consistent with that recovery for nitrogen but not for phosphate, where higher prices are suppressing demand [P001].

## Contradictions and alternative readings

- **Urea offtake growth rates differ slightly**: The executive summary states 84.9% growth [P001], while Table 1 states 84.9% and Table 3 states 84.9% [P003][P004]. The March 2026 review projected April urea offtake at 390 thousand tonnes [P017]; actual was 463 thousand tonnes—a 19% overshoot, suggesting demand is stronger than projected.
- **Kharif projections were revised sharply upward** between March and April reviews: urea availability +236 kt, closing stock +91 kt; DAP availability +56 kt. This reflects both higher actual April production/offtake and added import assumptions [P005][P017].
- **DAP import dependency is a key uncertainty**: The March review assumed zero DAP imports for Kharif [P017]; the April review added 55 kt [P005]. If imports slip, the projected 17 kt closing stock could turn negative.
- **The annual review's long-term projections show structural phosphate deficit**: For 2025-26, nitrogen is projected at -140 kt deficit and phosphate at -300 kt deficit [P034]. This contrasts with the seasonal Kharif projection showing urea surplus, reflecting that the annual figures include Rabi season demand.

## Unknowns

- **Gas supply reliability**: The NFDC repeatedly conditions DAP and urea projections on "smooth gas supply" and "full capacity" operation [P002][P005]. Actual gas availability is not quantified in the evidence.
- **Import timing and volumes**: Only 55 kt of DAP imports are scheduled (Jun-Jul) [P005]; whether these arrive on time is unknown.
- **Offtake sustainability**: April's 84.9% urea offtake surge may reflect restocking or one-off factors; the May-September projections assume 500-784 kt monthly offtake [P005].
- **Price elasticity**: DAP offtake fell 10.8% despite only a 2.9% monthly price rise; the annual review notes a 5% GST on DAP imports "disturbed the level playing field" [P023]. The demand response to further price increases is uncertain.
- **FFC Port Qasim status**: The March review assumed this plant "will remain shutdown during entire Kharif" [P017]; the April review does not state this assumption, yet production figures differ.

## Monitoring

- **NFDC monthly review**: Rerun when the May 2026 review is captured. New evidence that changes the answer: (a) actual May urea/DAP offtake versus the 500/94 kt projections [P005]; (b) whether DAP imports of 35 kt materialized in June; (c) any revision to Kharif closing stock estimates; (d) gas supply or plant shutdown announcements. If May urea offtake falls well below 500 kt, the surplus narrative strengthens; if DAP imports slip, the tightness narrative strengthens.
- **NFDC annual review**: Rerun when the FY2025-26 annual review is captured. New evidence: full-year production, import, and offtake actuals versus the projections in [P034]; confirmation of whether the projected nitrogen deficit (-140 kt) and phosphate deficit (-300 kt) materialized; any policy changes on gas pricing or GST.
monitors: NFDC monthly review: monthly; rerun when a later official review is captured

sections.title: Demand and affordability
sections.question: What is driving fertilizer demand and farmer affordability, what do product mix, crop economics and recent company commentary show, and which demand assumptions remain unverified?
sections.answer:
## Direct answer

Fertilizer demand in Pakistan is being driven by a sharp recovery in urea offtake (+84.9% YoY in April 2026) supported by improved farmer economics, while DAP demand is contracting (-10.8% YoY) due to high prices. Farmer affordability is being squeezed by rising fertilizer prices against mixed crop returns—wheat and paddy prices fell while fertilizer costs rose, worsening the crop-to-fertilizer exchange ratio. Product mix is shifting toward nitrogen (urea) and away from phosphate (DAP), with companies reporting market share shifts driven by pricing and gas cost structures. Unverified assumptions include the durability of the urea demand recovery, the impact of institutional credit expansion, and whether weather conditions remain favorable.

## What changed

- **Urea offtake surged** 84.9% YoY in April 2026 to 463 KT, after declining 24% in April 2025 [P001][P003].
- **DAP offtake fell** 10.8% YoY to 85 KT, attributed to higher prices [P001][P003].
- **All domestic fertilizer prices rose** month-on-month in April 2026; DAP up 2.9%, SOP up 6.0% [P006].
- **DAP international prices spiked** 39% YTD per Engro, with trade route disruptions [P066].
- **FFC urea market share rose** to 56% (from 48%), while Engro's fell to 21% (from 29%) [P052][P065].
- **Wheat support price announced** at PKR 3,500/maund (Punjab), with open market at PKR 3,700–4,650 [P064].

## Decisive evidence

| Claim | Evidence | Source |
|-------|----------|--------|
| Urea offtake +84.9% YoY in April 2026 | "Urea offtake was 463 thousand tonnes which increased by 84.9 per cent" | [P001] |
| DAP offtake -10.8% YoY in April 2026 | "DAP offtake was 85 thousand tonnes which decreased by 10.8 per cent" | [P001] |
| Phosphate decline due to higher prices | "Phosphate offtake decreased by 5 per cent which is mainly attributed to its higher prices" | [P001] |
| All fertilizer prices rose in April 2026 | "Prices of all fertilizer products increased during month under review compared with March 2026" | [P006] |
| DAP retail price Rs. 14,675/bag in April 2026 | "average price of urea (sona), urea (other) and DAP was Rs. 4,535, Rs. 4,398 and Rs. 14,675 per 50 kg bag" | [P006] |
| Wheat-to-urea exchange ratio worsened 56.6% | "Kg required to buy 1 kg of N from Urea: 2.22 → 3.48 (market price), +56.6%" | [P026] |
| Paddy-to-urea exchange ratio worsened ~71% | "IRRI: 2.08 → 3.57 (+71.4%); Basmati: 1.21 → 2.09 (+71.7%)" | [P026] |
| DAP prices surged PKR 14,000→16,000/bag | "DAP prices surging from PKR 14,000 to PKR 16,000/bag significantly compressed demand" | [P064] |
| FFC urea share rose to 56% | "FFC Share Increased to 56% (48% SPLY)" | [P052] |
| Engro share fell due to gas cost structure | "EFERT's market share declined due to planned pricing actions - necessitated by a comparatively higher gas cost structure" | [P065] |
| DAP international prices +39% YTD | "DAP international Price (USD/MT): 39% Increase YTD" | [P066] |
| 2025-26 urea demand estimate +17.4% | "offtake of urea is estimated to increase by 17.4 per cent" | [P023] |
| 2025-26 DAP demand estimate -2.7% | "DAP offtake is expected to decrease slightly by 2.7 per cent mainly due its high prices" | [P023] |

## Interpretation

**Demand drivers:** The April 2026 urea surge (+84.9%) follows a weak April 2025 (-24%), suggesting a rebound from a depressed base rather than purely organic growth. Engro attributes industry urea growth to "favorable farmer economics" [P065], citing wheat support prices and improved rice prices [P064]. However, NFDC data shows crop-to-fertilizer exchange ratios deteriorated sharply in 2024-25—wheat required 56.6% more kg to buy 1 kg of N, and paddy required ~71% more [P026]. This contradiction suggests the April 2026 surge may reflect restocking, pre-buying, or seasonal timing rather than sustained affordability improvement.

**Affordability:** Farmer affordability is under structural pressure. Wheat market prices fell from Rs. 3,369 to Rs. 2,217 per 40 kg (2023-24 to 2024-25) while urea prices rose [P025]. DAP at Rs. 14,675/bag in April 2026 is 18.7% above April 2025's Rs. 12,363 [P006]. Engro explicitly states DAP price increases "significantly compressed demand and impacted farmer affordability, particularly for smallholder farmers" [P064].

**Product mix:** The market is bifurcating—nitrogen demand is robust while phosphate demand contracts. NFDC projects urea offtake +17.4% but DAP -2.7% for 2025-26 [P023]. NFDC recommends promoting TSP, NP, and SSP as cheaper phosphate alternatives [P023]. Company data confirms this: FFC's DAP market share rose to 65% while Engro's fell to 13% [P053][P066], with Engro citing "elevated pricing" impacts.

**Company commentary:** FFC gained urea share (56%) and DAP share (65%) [P052][P053]. Engro lost share in both products, explicitly attributing urea share loss to "a comparatively higher gas cost structure" requiring pricing actions [P065]. Engro maintains large inventory (74% of industry urea inventory) positioning for "2H 2026 demand recovery" [P065].

## Contradictions and alternative readings

1. **"Favorable farmer economics" vs. deteriorating exchange ratios:** Engro claims favorable farmer economics drove demand [P065], but NFDC data shows crop-to-fertilizer ratios worsened 28-72% across crops in 2024-25 [P026]. The April 2026 surge may reflect a low base effect (April 2025 was -24% YoY) rather than genuine affordability improvement.

2. **DAP demand divergence:** NFDC reports DAP offtake -10.8% in April 2026 [P001], but Engro reports industry DAP sales +13% YTD [P066]. This may reflect Q1 pre-buying ahead of price increases, with Q2 sales down 30% [P066].

3. **Urea demand estimate vs. actual:** NFDC's 2025-26 estimate of +17.4% urea growth [P023] appears consistent with April's +84.9%, but this assumes the April pace sustains—unverified for the full year.

## Unknowns

1. **Sustainability of urea demand:** Whether April's surge reflects genuine farmer purchasing power or one-time restocking/pre-buying ahead of price increases.
2. **Credit impact:** Engro cites "projected increase in institutional agricultural credit" as supporting demand [P064], but no credit disbursement data is provided.
3. **Weather dependency:** Engro conditions demand recovery on "weather conditions remain favourable" [P064]—unverified for Kharif 2026.
4. **Gas cost structure:** Engro's higher gas costs are cited as a competitive disadvantage [P065], but specific gas price differentials are not quantified in company materials.
5. **DAP substitution:** Whether farmers shift to TSP/NP/SSP as NFDC recommends [P023] is not yet visible in April 2026 data (NP production 76 KT, SSP only 3.4 KT).

## Monitoring

| Monitor | What new evidence changes the answer | Where it arrives |
|---------|--------------------------------------|------------------|
| **NFDC monthly review** | If urea offtake sustains above +50% YoY for May-June 2026, the demand recovery is confirmed as structural; if it reverts to single digits, April was a base-effect artifact. DAP offtake trends will confirm or refute phosphate substitution. | NFDC monthly review (monthly) |
| **Issuer result briefings** | Q3 2026 briefings will reveal whether Engro's inventory drawdown and market share recovery materialize as projected, and whether FFC's share gains persist. Any commentary on gas pricing changes or credit disbursement would update affordability assumptions. | Issuer result briefings and material information (event-driven) |
monitors: Issuer result briefings and material information: event-driven

sections.title: Supply, gas and operating capacity
sections.question: What constrains domestic fertilizer supply today, how do gas allocation, RLNG prices, outages and capacity investments affect availability and risk, and what material contractual or reserve evidence is still missing?
sections.answer:
## Direct answer

Domestic fertilizer supply is constrained by gas allocation priorities, gas price levels, and plant operating reliability. The 2005 Natural Gas Allocation and Management Policy gives fertilizer plants second priority on the system and first priority on independent networks, but allocation volumes are set by the Federal Government, not guaranteed by the policy [P041], [P043]. Gas prices for fertilizer feed stock were unified at Rs 1,597/MMBTU on SNGPL/SSGC systems from February 2024, while Mari-system prices remained at Rs 580/MMBTU [P028]. RLNG prices are substantially higher—the July 2026 weighted average sale price was US$23.70/MMBTU for SNGPL and US$25.84/MMBTU for SSGC [P039]. Two plants (Agritech, Fatimafert) rely on RLNG, consuming 27,042 MMCF in 2024-25 [P036]. Outages are a recurring risk: Engro's Base plant had a forced 4-day shutdown in July 2026 [P070], [P071]. NFDC's Kharif 2026 outlook assumes all plants operate at full capacity, with urea closing stock of 574 thousand tonnes and DAP closing stock of only 17 thousand tonnes [P005]. Missing evidence includes current gas allocation letters, gas sales agreements, plant-level capacity investment plans, and reserve data.

## What changed

- **Gas prices**: Feed gas for fertilizer on SNGPL/SSGC systems rose from Rs 580 to Rs 1,597/MMBTU effective February 1, 2024, and remained at that level through January 2025 (latest data) [P028]. Mari-system feed gas stayed at Rs 580/MMBTU [P028].
- **Subsidy**: Implicit feed-gas subsidy fell from Rs 121.20 billion in 2023-24 to Rs 84.49 billion in 2024-25 (-30.3%), with SNGPL and SSGC subsidies eliminated entirely [P028].
- **Gas consumption**: Total fertilizer gas consumption rose from 274,449 MMCF in 2023-24 to 281,153 MMCF in 2024-25 (+2.4%) [P035], [P036].
- **RLNG reliance**: Agritech and Fatimafert consumed 27,042 MMCF of RLNG in 2024-25, with Agritech showing a sharp January 2025 dip (220 MMCF feed vs ~750-800 typical) [P036].
- **Outage**: Engro Base plant forced outage July 3-10, 2026 (~4 days) [P070], [P071].
- **Urea offtake**: April 2026 urea offtake surged 84.9% year-on-year to 463 thousand tonnes [P003].

## Decisive evidence

| Claim | Evidence | Source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Fertilizer has second priority on system gas, first on independent networks | Policy priority order: Domestic/Commercial first; Fertilizer and Industrial process gas second; independent network: Fertilizer first | [P043] |
| Fertilizer gas allocation is discretionary, not guaranteed | "Gas allocation for the Fertilizer Sector will be made by the Federal Government keeping in view the domestic needs and gas supply position" | [P041] |
| Feed gas price on SNGPL/SSGC = Rs 1,597/MMBTU since Feb 2024 | Price table shows Rs 1,597 for all SNGPL/SSGC feed stock from 01-02-2024 through 01-01-2025 | [P028] |
| Mari-system feed gas = Rs 580/MMBTU | Price table shows Rs 580 for EFERT, FFC, Fatima on Mari system | [P028] |
| RLNG July 2026 price = US$23.70 (SNGPL) / US$25.84 (SSGC) per MMBTU | Weighted average sale price computation | [P039] |
| RLNG price includes fertilizer diversion adjustment | "Price differential for RLNG diversion to Fertilizer Sector: 0.5744" | [P039] |
| Agritech and Fatimafert use RLNG | 2024-25 gas consumption: Agritech 8,636 feed + 2,033 fuel; Fatimafert 13,628 feed + 2,745 fuel (MMCF) | [P036] |
| Engro Base plant forced outage July 2026 | Disclosure: shutdown for unscheduled maintenance, ~4 days | [P070] |
| Engro Base plant resumed July 10, 2026 | Resumption disclosure | [P071] |
| Kharif 2026 assumes full-capacity operation | "It is assumed that all plants will remain operational" | [P005] |
| Kharif 2026 DAP closing stock thin at 17 thousand tonnes | Supply/demand projection table | [P005] |
| Feed-gas subsidy fell 30.3% in 2024-25 | Rs 121.20 bn (2023-24) to Rs 84.49 bn (2024-25) | [P028] |

## Interpretation

The policy framework prioritizes fertilizer but gives the government discretion over allocation volumes, creating structural uncertainty. The price gap between Mari-system gas (Rs 580) and SNGPL/SSGC gas (Rs 1,597) means plants on different systems face very different cost structures. RLNG-dependent plants face prices roughly 40 times higher than Mari-system feed gas (US$23.70 vs ~Rs 580/MMBTU equivalent), making their economics highly sensitive to international LNG prices. The July 2026 RLNG price of US$23.70/MMBTU is elevated, and the fertilizer diversion adjustment (US$0.5744) adds a further cost. The subsidy reduction signals fiscal pressure, potentially affecting future gas pricing decisions. The thin DAP closing stock projection (17 thousand tonnes) indicates low inventory resilience; any supply disruption could create shortages. The Engro outage, though brief, demonstrates that even short forced shutdowns matter when inventories are tight. NFDC's assumption of full-capacity operation is an assumption, not a commitment—actual availability depends on gas supply continuity and plant reliability.

## Contradictions and alternative readings

- **Policy vs. practice**: The 2005 policy gives fertilizer second priority, but the same policy allows the Federal Government to determine fertilizer allocations "keeping in view the domestic needs and gas supply position" [P041]. This discretion could override the stated priority in practice.
- **Price data lag**: The gas price table in [P028] ends at January 2025, while RLNG prices are current to July 2026. Whether SNGPL/SSGC feed gas prices changed after January 2025 is unknown.
- **Subsidy interpretation**: The "implicit subsidy" is an NFDC estimate, not an actual budgetary transfer. The elimination of SNGPL/SSGC subsidies could reflect either policy change or accounting methodology.
- **Outage impact**: The Engro disclosure does not state production loss or market impact. A 4-day outage may be immaterial if inventory buffers exist, but NFDC's thin closing stock projections suggest otherwise.
- **RLNG price composition**: The July 2026 price includes provisional cost-of-supply figures and volume adjustments subject to later scrutiny [P039], so the final price may differ.

## Unknowns

- **Current gas allocation volumes**: No evidence of 2025-26 or 2026-27 allocation letters to individual fertilizer plants.
- **Gas sales agreements**: Terms, durations, and curtailment provisions of GSAs between utilities and fertilizer plants are not in the evidence.
- **Capacity investments**: No evidence of planned expansions, debottlenecking, or new plants.
- **Reserve data**: The 2005 policy cites 32 TCF recoverable reserves and a 23-year R/P ratio [P040], but no updated reserve figures are provided.
- **Post-January 2025 feed gas prices**: Whether SNGPL/SSGC or Mari-system prices changed after the last data point.
- **RLNG contract terms**: The July 2026 computation shows only PLL cargos (5, at DES US$18.98/MMBTU); PSO cargos are absent, and the underlying contract formulas are not disclosed [P039].
- **Plant-level production capacity**: Actual nameplate capacities and current utilization rates are not stated.

## Monitoring

| Monitor | What new evidence changes the answer | Where it arrives |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| OGRA prices (monthly) | A change in SNGPL/SSGC feed gas price from Rs 1,597/MMBTU, or a change in Mari-system price from Rs 580/MMBTU, would alter cost competitiveness. A sustained drop in RLNG price would improve RLNG-dependent plant economics. | OGRA monthly price notifications |
| Gas instruments and issuer operating events (event-driven) | A new gas allocation letter, GSA signing, or curtailment notice would confirm or change actual supply availability. A new outage disclosure (beyond Engro's July 2026 event) would signal reliability risk. | PSX disclosures by Engro and other listed fertilizer issuers; Petroleum Division notifications |
| NFDC monthly review (monthly) | Monthly production, offtake, and inventory data would confirm whether Kharif 2026 projections (urea closing 574 kt, DAP closing 17 kt) are tracking or deteriorating. A revision to the "all plants operational" assumption would directly change supply risk. | NFDC monthly Fertilizer Review publications |
monitors: Gas instruments and issuer operating events: event-driven

sections.title: Price and margin transmission
sections.question: How are fertilizer prices, gas costs, imports, product mix and company actions transmitting into sector margins, and which apparent relationships are evidence versus inference?
sections.answer:
## Direct answer

Fertilizer prices, gas costs, imports, product mix, and company actions are transmitting into sector margins through three distinct channels: (1) **price-cost squeeze on imported products**—DAP and other phosphate-based fertilizers face rising international prices and elevated import costs, compressing margins for import-dependent players; (2) **gas cost-driven volume discipline**—Engro explicitly reduced urea sales volumes to preserve margins amid higher gas costs, accepting revenue decline to maintain gross margin; (3) **subsidy withdrawal shifting cost burden**—feed gas subsidy fell from Rs. 121.20 billion to Rs. 84.49 billion year-on-year, transferring cost to producers. Evidence supports price transmission; margin causation is partly inference.

## What changed

- **April 2026 vs March 2026**: All domestic fertilizer prices rose—urea (sona) +1.8%, DAP +2.9%, NP +2.4%, SSP +3.8%, SOP +6.0%, NPK +2.0%, CAN +1.1% [P001][P006].
- **April 2026 vs April 2025**: DAP price up from Rs. 12,363 to Rs. 14,675 per bag (+18.7%); NP up from Rs. 7,701 to Rs. 9,162 (+19.0%); SSP up from Rs. 2,964 to Rs. 3,438 (+16.0%) [P006].
- **International prices**: Urea (Middle East) rose from US$745-780 (early April) to US$830-900 (late April); DAP (Morocco) from US$760-845 to US$821-950 [P007].
- **Gas prices**: Feed gas for SNGPL system rose from Rs. 580 to Rs. 1,597/MMBTU effective 01-02-2024, holding through 2025 [P028]. RLNG July 2026: US$23.70/MMBTU (SNGPL transmission) [P039].
- **Subsidy**: Feed gas subsidy fell 30.3% to Rs. 84.49 billion in 2024-25; EFERT and FFBL subsidies eliminated entirely [P028].
- **Company results**: FFC H1'26 revenue +28%, gross profit +19%, net profit +9% [P054]. EFERT Q2'26 revenue -34%, profit -32%; H1'26 revenue -12%, profit -16% [P067][P068].

## Decisive evidence

| Claim | Evidence | Source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| All domestic fertilizer prices rose in April 2026 vs March 2026 | Urea +1.8%, DAP +2.9%, NP +2.4%, SSP +3.8%, SOP +6.0%, NPK +2.0%, CAN +1.1% | [P001][P006] |
| DAP price rose 18.7% year-on-year (April 2026 vs April 2025) | Rs. 14,675 vs Rs. 12,363 per 50kg bag | [P006] |
| International urea and DAP prices rose through April 2026 | Urea ME: US$745-780 → US$830-900; DAP Morocco: US$760-845 → US$821-950 | [P007] |
| Feed gas price for SNGPL system is Rs. 1,597/MMBTU | Effective 01-02-2024, unchanged through 01-01-2025 | [P028] |
| Feed gas subsidy fell 30.3% to Rs. 84.49 billion in 2024-25 | Rs. 121.20 billion in 2023-24; EFERT and FFBL subsidies eliminated | [P028] |
| RLNG price for July 2026 is US$23.70/MMBTU (SNGPL) | Weighted average sale price without GST | [P039] |
| FFC H1'26: revenue +28%, gross profit +19%, net profit +9% | PKR 199.6bn, 63.7bn, 41.8bn respectively | [P054] |
| FFC fertilizer operations profit: PKR 22.9bn (55% of net profit) | Investment + dividend income = 45% of net profit | [P055] |
| EFERT H1'26: revenue -12%, profit -16% | Lower urea volumes (-154KT) and DAP volumes (-14KT) | [P067][P068] |
| EFERT maintained 33% gross margin despite revenue decline | "Gross Margin has been maintained at 33%" | [P068] |
| EFERT reduced urea volumes to preserve margins | "Planned pricing actions to preserve margins amid a higher gas cost structure" | [P068] |
| FFC stock-in-trade rose to PKR 64.4bn from PKR 38.2bn | "Higher DAP Inventory" | [P056] |
| Phosphate offtake fell 5% in April 2026 | "Mainly attributed to its higher prices" | [P001] |

## Interpretation

**Evidence-based relationships:**

1. **International-to-domestic price transmission**: International urea and DAP prices rose through April 2026 [P007], and domestic prices rose concurrently [P006]. The NFDC attributes phosphate offtake decline to higher prices [P001]. This is direct evidence of price pass-through.

2. **Gas cost → volume response**: EFERT explicitly states it reduced urea sales volumes (down 154KT) as "planned pricing actions to preserve margins amid a higher gas cost structure" [P068]. This is direct evidence of gas costs driving company behavior.

3. **Subsidy withdrawal → cost transfer**: Feed gas subsidy fell from Rs. 121.20 to Rs. 84.49 billion [P028]. This is evidence of reduced government support, but the margin impact on individual companies requires company-level data.

4. **Product mix divergence**: Urea offtake rose 84.9% while DAP offtake fell 10.8% in April 2026 [P001]. This divergence—with urea prices rising modestly (+1.8%) and DAP prices rising sharply (+2.9%)—suggests demand destruction in phosphates.

**Inference-based relationships:**

1. **Margin compression for importers**: The evidence shows DAP import prices (Ex-Karachi: Rs. 13,641-16,762/bag) overlap with domestic retail prices (Rs. 14,675 average) [P006][P007]. Inferring thin or negative margins for importers is reasonable but not directly evidenced—no importer margin data is provided.

2. **Gas cost → margin squeeze**: EFERT's gross margin held at 33% despite higher gas costs [P068], suggesting the company absorbed costs through volume reduction rather than margin erosion. Whether this is sustainable is inference.

3. **FFC's profitability composition**: Fertilizer operations contributed only 55% of FFC's net profit; investment and dividend income contributed 45% [P055]. Inferring that FFC's fertilizer margins are weak relative to financial income is plausible but requires cost data not provided.

## Contradictions and alternative readings

1. **FFC vs EFERT divergence**: FFC grew revenue +28% and profit +9% [P054], while EFERT declined -12% and -16% [P067]. Both face similar gas cost structures (Mari gas at Rs. 580/MMBTU) [P028]. Alternative reading: FFC's growth may reflect DAP inventory gains (stock-in-trade up from Rs. 38.2bn to Rs. 64.4bn) [P056], not operational efficiency. FFC's "higher DAP inventory" could be speculative stocking ahead of price increases.

2. **Urea offtake surge vs price rise**: Urea offtake rose 84.9% while prices rose only 1.8% [P001][P006]. Alternative reading: the offtake surge may reflect pre-Kharif stocking or supply availability, not price-driven demand. The NFDC does not explain the surge.

3. **Subsidy elimination for EFERT/FFBL**: Table 42 shows EFERT and FFBL subsidies at zero in 2024-25 [P028]. Yet EFERT maintained 33% gross margin [P068]. Alternative reading: EFERT's margin maintenance may reflect one-off gains (SIDC provision remeasurement) rather than sustainable operations [P068].

4. **RLNG price level**: July 2026 RLNG at US$23.70/MMBTU [P039] is far above the Rs. 1,597/MMBTU feed gas price [P028]. Companies using RLNG (Agritech, Fatimafert) face structurally higher costs, but their margins are not separately reported in the evidence.

## Unknowns

1. **Company-level gas costs**: The evidence provides regulated gas prices [P028] but not actual contracted prices or volumes per company for 2026.
2. **Importer margins**: No data on importers' cost structures or realized margins.
3. **FFC's DAP inventory economics**: Whether the PKR 64.4bn inventory reflects higher volumes or higher prices is unspecified [P056].
4. **EFERT's one-off gain magnitude**: The SIDC provision remeasurement gain is mentioned but not quantified [P068].
5. **Urea offtake surge drivers**: No explanation for the 84.9% increase [P001].
6. **Current subsidy status**: The subsidy data covers 2024-25 [P028]; whether the Rs. 84.49 billion level persists into 2025-26 or 2026-27 is unknown.

## Monitoring

| Monitor | What new evidence changes the answer | Where it arrives |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **NFDC monthly prices** | If DAP domestic prices rise faster than international prices, margins for importers may be expanding; if slower, compression. If urea prices rise while offtake falls, demand destruction is occurring. | NFDC Fertilizer Review, monthly |
| **OGRA gas prices** | If feed gas prices rise above Rs. 1,597/MMBTU, EFERT's margin maintenance becomes unsustainable. If RLNG prices fall, Agritech/Fatimafert margins improve. | OGRA notifications, monthly |
| **Issuer results (FFC, EFERT)** | Q3'26 results will reveal whether EFERT's 33% gross margin held, whether FFC's DAP inventory was monetized profitably, and whether fertilizer operations' profit share changed. | Corporate briefings, quarterly |
| **Issuer briefings** | Management commentary on gas cost outlook, pricing strategy, and import plans will clarify whether volume reduction is structural or temporary. | Corporate briefings, event-driven |

New evidence from NFDC monthly reviews would change the price transmission analysis directly. New OGRA gas price notifications would change the cost-side analysis. Issuer results would confirm or refute the inference that margins are being preserved through volume sacrifice rather than price recovery.

Issuer results and briefings: quarterly or event-driven

sections.title: FFC operations and earnings
sections.question: What changed in FFC's latest operating and financial performance, what explains the movement, and which claims cannot yet be verified without the full Q2 notes?
sections.answer:
## Direct answer

FFC's H1 2026 (six months ended June 30, 2026) shows a 28% revenue increase to PKR 199.6 billion, a 9% net profit increase to PKR 41.8 billion, and EPS of PKR 29.08 versus PKR 27.02 in H1 2025 [P047]. The movement is driven by higher urea and DAP sales volumes, improved urea market share (56% vs 48%), and PKR 28.2 billion in other income [P044][P045][P052]. However, the standalone Q2 (three months ended June 30, 2026) actually shows a slight profit decline: PKR 24.37 billion versus PKR 25.17 billion in Q2 2025 [P047]. Several claims—including the composition of other income, the PIA Equity investment rationale, and segment-level cost drivers—cannot be verified without the full Q2 notes.

## What changed

**Operational changes (H1 2026 vs H1 2025):**
- Prilled urea production: 1,262 KT, up 3% [P044]
- Granular urea production: 155 KT, down from 192 KT (19% decline) [P044]
- Sona DAP production: 369 KT, down 6% [P044]
- Urea offtake: 1,404 KT vs 1,122 KT (25% increase) [P045][P052]
- DAP sales (incl. imported): 318 KT vs 288 KT (11% increase) [P045][P053]
- Urea market share: 56% vs 48% [P045][P052]
- DAP market share: 65-66% vs 63% [P045][P053]

**Financial changes (H1 2026 vs H1 2025):**
- Revenue: PKR 199.6B vs PKR 155.4B (+28%) [P047][P054]
- Gross profit: PKR 63.7B vs PKR 53.6B (+19%) [P047][P054]
- Other income: PKR 28.2B vs PKR 28.2B (flat) [P047][P054]
- Net profit: PKR 41.8B vs PKR 38.5B (+9%) [P047][P054]
- EPS: PKR 29.08 vs PKR 27.02 [P047]
- Consolidated PAT: PKR 42.4B, +12% YoY [P045][P050]

**Balance sheet changes (June 30, 2026 vs Dec 31, 2025):**
- Long-term borrowings: PKR 72.4B vs PKR 50.3B (+44%) [P046]
- Stock in trade: PKR 64.4B vs PKR 38.2B (+68%) [P046]
- Long-term investments: PKR 109.8B vs PKR 79.1B (+39%) [P046]
- Property, plant and equipment: PKR 96.6B vs PKR 76.6B (+26%) [P046]

**Cash flow changes (H1 2026 vs H1 2025):**
- Operating cash flow: PKR 29.8B vs (PKR 33.5B) [P048]
- Fixed capital expenditure: PKR 23.6B vs PKR 7.2B (3.3x increase) [P048]
- PIA Equity investment + advance: PKR 30.6B combined [P048]

## Decisive evidence

| Claim | Evidence | Source |
|-------|----------|--------|
| Revenue up 28% YoY to PKR 199.6B | Turnover-net H1 2026: 199,613,700 vs 155,448,542 | [P047] |
| Net profit up 9% YoY to PKR 41.8B | Profit for period: 41,845,807 vs 38,451,802 | [P047] |
| Q2 standalone profit declined YoY | Q2 2026: 24,368,981 vs Q2 2025: 25,173,980 | [P047] |
| Urea sales up 25% to 1,404 KT | Sales table: 1,404 vs 1,122 KT | [P052] |
| Urea market share 56% vs 48% | Market share slide | [P052] |
| DAP sales up 11% to 318 KT | Sales table: 318 vs 288 KT | [P053] |
| DAP production down 6% | 369 KT vs prior year; gas curtailment and phosphoric acid shortage | [P044] |
| Other income PKR 28.2B, flat YoY | Other income line: 28,238,137 vs 28,161,501 | [P047] |
| PIA Equity investment PKR 30.6B | Investment 1,699,500 + advance 28,900,959 | [P048] |
| Long-term borrowings up PKR 22.1B | 72,375,000 vs 50,250,000 | [P046] |

## Interpretation

The H1 2026 results reflect a volume-led recovery. Urea offtake growth of 25% against production growth of only 3% for prilled urea indicates FFC drew down inventory or increased imports to meet demand—consistent with stock-in-trade rising from PKR 38.2B to PKR 64.4B [P046]. The market share gain from 48% to 56% suggests competitors lost share, though the evidence does not identify which competitors or why.

The flat other income (PKR 28.2B in both periods) is notable: despite higher cash generation and larger short-term investment balances, other income did not grow. This may reflect lower yields or a shift in investment composition, but the notes are not provided.

The Q2 standalone profit decline (PKR 24.37B vs PKR 25.17B) despite higher revenue (PKR 104.3B vs PKR 91.8B) indicates margin compression in Q2 specifically. Gross margin fell from 33.7% to 33.1% in Q2, and other income fell from PKR 20.7B to PKR 17.6B [P047]. The full-year H1 improvement is therefore driven primarily by Q1 performance.

The PKR 30.6B PIA Equity investment and advance is the largest single investing outflow and explains the shift from net cash generation of PKR 4.0B in H1 2025 to net cash usage of PKR 38.1B in H1 2026 [P048]. This was funded partly by PKR 30.0B in new long-term borrowings [P048].

## Contradictions and alternative readings

1. **Market share discrepancy**: The announcement text states DAP market share "registered a growth of 3% to 66%" [P045], while the corporate briefing slide states 65% (63% SPLY) [P053]. The briefing also shows a 2026 market share of 65% [P053]. This is a 1-percentage-point discrepancy between sources.

2. **Q2 vs H1 narrative**: The announcement emphasizes "higher urea sales during the second quarter compared with the first quarter of 2026" [P044], yet Q2 standalone profit was lower than Q2 2025. The H1 improvement masks Q2 weakness.

3. **Production vs sales mismatch**: Prilled urea production rose only 3% but sales rose 25%. The announcement attributes this to "focused marketing and distribution efforts" [P044], but inventory drawdown is the more plausible mechanical explanation given the balance sheet data.

4. **"Control over operating costs" claim**: The announcement claims cost control [P045], but distribution costs rose from PKR 14.8B to PKR 17.7B (+20%) [P047], roughly in line with revenue growth. This claim is not supported by the financial statements.

## Unknowns

Without the full Q2 notes, the following cannot be verified:

1. **Composition of other income**: The PKR 28.2B includes investment income, but the split between dividends, interest, and capital gains is not disclosed in the provided pages.

2. **PIA Equity investment details**: The rationale, valuation, and expected returns of the PKR 30.6B investment and advance are not explained.

3. **Segment-level cost drivers**: The 34% increase in cost of sales (PKR 135.9B vs PKR 101.8B) [P047] is attributed to volumes, but input price effects (gas, phosphoric acid) are not quantified.

4. **Tax rate movement**: The effective tax rate fell from 34.6% to 35.8% in H1 (23,315,408/65,161,215 vs 20,334,426/58,786,228), but the drivers are not disclosed.

5. **Related-party transactions**: The Agritech Limited investment (PKR 433M) and loan (PKR 104M) [P048] lack context.

6. **Contingencies and commitments**: The balance sheet references this line [P046] but no details are provided.

7. **Borrowing terms**: The PKR 30.0B drawdown [P048] terms, maturity, and purpose are not disclosed.

## Monitoring

| Monitor | What new evidence changes the answer | Where it arrives |
|---------|--------------------------------------|------------------|
| FFC Q2 2026 full report (quarterly) | Would confirm other income composition, PIA Equity details, segment costs, tax reconciliation, and borrowing terms | FFC quarterly report transmitted through PUCARS [P045] |
| FFC Q3 2026 results (event-driven) | Would show whether Q2 margin compression continued or reversed, and whether PIA Equity investment yields returns | FFC results announcement to PSX/SECP |
| FFC corporate briefing for Q2 (event-driven) | Would provide management commentary on Q2 profit decline and PIA Equity rationale | FFC investor briefing materials |
| FFC material information disclosures (event-driven) | Any price-sensitive information on PIA Equity, gas supply, or phosphoric acid contracts | FFC announcements to PSX/SECP |

The Q2 full report is the critical missing document. It is expected to be transmitted "through PUCARS separately, within specified time" [P045], which would resolve most unknowns listed above.
monitors: FFC results, reports, briefings and material information: event-driven; formal reports: quarterly

sections.title: FFC capital allocation and Agritech exposure
sections.question: What is FFC investing in, how material is its Agritech exposure, what are the accounting and financing terms, and what remains uncertain about capital allocation?
sections.answer:
## Direct answer

FFC is investing across four main areas: (1) core fertilizer operations, including fixed capital expenditure of PKR 17.1 billion in Q1 2026; (2) Agritech Limited (AGL), where it holds a 37.36% equity stake at cost of PKR 7.31 billion plus a running finance facility; (3) financial assets, with PKR 284.2 billion in total investments (PKR 174.4 billion short-term); and (4) group expansion, including acquiring full control of FFBL Power Company Limited (FPCL) via share issuance. Agritech exposure is material but modest relative to total investments: PKR 7.31 billion equity at cost plus PKR 1.32 billion loan against PKR 284.2 billion total investments. Accounting terms include cost-based carrying for AGL equity, KIBOR-linked preference shares, and a loan at weighted average cost of debt plus 0.10%. Financing includes KIBOR-linked borrowings and a share-for-share FPCL acquisition. Uncertainty centers on regulatory approvals for FPCL, GIDC litigation, and AGL's redemption/conversion options.

## What changed

- **FPCL control**: Shareholders approved acquiring 214.7 million FPCL shares (25%) from Fauji Foundation via issuing 15.9 million FFC shares; effective January 2026, FFC gained full control [P098][P100].
- **AGL investment increase**: FFC invested PKR 5.18 billion in AGL during 2025, raising equity stake to 37.36%; cost rose from PKR 4.86 billion to PKR 7.31 billion [P097][P100].
- **AGL loan**: New running finance facility of PKR 1.32 billion extended to AGL in 2025 (nil in 2024) [P099].
- **Long-term borrowings**: Rose from PKR 61.3 billion (Dec 2025) to PKR 85.8 billion (Jun 2026); debt-to-equity shifted from 27:73 to 32:68 [P056].
- **Fixed capex**: Q1 2026 fixed capital expenditure of PKR 17.1 billion versus PKR 5.0 billion in Q1 2025 [P076].

## Decisive evidence

| Claim | Evidence | Source |
|-------|----------|--------|
| AGL equity stake 37.36% at year-end 2025; PKR 5.18B additional investment | "aggregate equity stake increasing to 37.36% at year end"; "additional investment of PKR 5.18 billion" | [P100] |
| AGL investment at cost PKR 7.31B (2025) vs PKR 4.86B (2024) | "Investment at cost 7,307,542" vs "4,855,105" | [P097] |
| AGL running finance PKR 1.32B at WACC + 0.10% | "running finance facility... markup arrangement at the Company's weighted average cost of debt plus 0.10% per annum"; "1,318,294" | [P099] |
| AGL preference shares at KIBOR + 4.00%, redeemable at AGL option | "carry dividend at KIBOR + 4.00% and can be redeemed, in full or in part, at the option of AGL" | [P098] |
| Total investments PKR 284.2B (ST: PKR 174.4B) | "Investments PKR 284.2 Bn (ST: PKR 174.4 Bn)" | [P056] |
| Q1 2026 fixed capex PKR 17.1B | "Fixed capital expenditure (17,139,988)" | [P076] |
| FPCL acquisition via 15.9M FFC shares for 214.7M FPCL shares | "acquisition of 214,687,500 ordinary voting shares... against a consideration to issue 15,914,566 ordinary shares" | [P098] |
| Long-term borrowings PKR 85.8B; debt-to-equity 32:68 | "Long term Borrowings PKR 85.8 Bn"; "Debt to Equity 32% : 68%" | [P056] |
| Borrowings at 3M/6M KIBOR ± 0.5%; TERF at 2.5–3.5% | "mark-up ranging between 3 month KIBOR plus 0.5% to 6 month KIBOR plus 0.5%"; "TERF facilities... 2.5% to 3.5%" | [P077] |
| GIDC payable PKR 84.98B; stay granted; no payments made | "amount payable... 84,977,267 thousand"; "no payments were made... due to the stay" | [P077] |

## Interpretation

FFC's capital allocation is dominated by financial assets (PKR 284.2 billion investments) rather than Agritech. AGL exposure comprises three instruments: equity at cost (PKR 7.31 billion), preference shares (875.9 million shares at KIBOR + 4%), and a running finance facility (PKR 1.32 billion). Combined, these represent roughly 3% of total investments. The strategic rationale stated is "ensuring reliable supply of urea and food security" [P100]. Financing for expansion relies on KIBOR-linked debt (PKR 85.8 billion long-term) and equity issuance for FPCL. The Q1 2026 capex surge (PKR 17.1 billion) suggests significant fixed asset investment, likely in fertilizer operations given segment data showing PKR 16.5 billion in fertilizer segment capex [P078].

## Contradictions and alternative readings

- **AGL materiality**: The Chairman's Review emphasizes AGL as "strategically important" [P100], yet financial statements show it as a small fraction of investments. The strategic narrative may overstate financial materiality.
- **Investment income decline**: Group investment income fell to PKR 18.7 billion from PKR 27 billion in 2024 [P100], while FFC standalone investment income was PKR 5.3 billion in H1 2026 versus PKR 6.1 billion in H1 2025 [P055]. This suggests diminishing returns on the large investment portfolio.
- **FPCL valuation**: The share-for-share exchange implies a specific valuation, but the packet does not disclose the exchange ratio basis or independent valuation.
- **GIDC treatment**: The Group has not accounted for late payment surcharge despite the Supreme Court upholding the GIDC Act, relying on a Sindh High Court stay now transferred to a Civil Judge [P077]. This is a contested position.

## Unknowns

- **FPCL regulatory approvals**: The share issuance for FPCL control requires "necessary regulatory approvals" not yet obtained as of year-end [P098].
- **AGL redemption timing**: Preference shares are redeemable "at the option of AGL" — timing and amount are undisclosed [P098].
- **GIDC resolution**: The matter transferred to Civil Judge, Karachi; outcome and payment schedule (48 installments per government order) remain uncertain [P077].
- **Capex destination**: Q1 2026 fixed capex of PKR 17.1 billion is not broken down by project in the cash flow statement; segment data shows PKR 16.5 billion in fertilizer segment [P076][P078].
- **Future AGL investment**: Whether FFC will further increase its stake beyond 37.36% is not stated.

## Monitoring

| Monitor | New evidence that changes answer | Where it arrives |
|---------|----------------------------------|------------------|
| FPCL regulatory approvals and share issuance completion | Approval or rejection changes control consolidation and share count | FFC formal reports (quarterly); event-driven filings |
| AGL equity stake changes or additional investment | Further stake increases change materiality calculation | FFC and Agritech filings; event-driven; formal reports quarterly |
| AGL preference share redemption or conversion | Redemption changes cash flows and investment composition | FFC and Agritech filings; event-driven |
| GIDC court decision or payment resumption | Ruling changes liability recognition and cash outflows | FFC formal reports (quarterly); event-driven |
| Fixed capex project disclosures | Breakdown reveals whether capex is fertilizer capacity, diversification, or maintenance | FFC formal reports (quarterly); event-driven project disclosures |
| Long-term borrowing drawdowns and terms | New facilities change leverage and financing costs | FFC formal reports (quarterly) |
| AGL loan facility usage and repayment | Utilization indicates AGL cash burn and FFC support level | FFC and Agritech filings; event-driven; formal reports quarterly |
monitors: FFC and Agritech filings, investment changes and project disclosures: event-driven; formal reports: quarterly

sections.title: EFERT company view
sections.question: What changed in EFERT's performance, volumes, projects, operations and leadership, what appears to drive those changes, and what remains unavailable pending the full Q2 report?
sections.answer:
## Direct answer

EFERT's Q2 2026 (quarter ended June 30, 2026) shows broad declines: revenue down 34% YoY, profit down 32%, EPS down from PKR 4.17 to PKR 2.85. Volumes fell sharply in both urea (Engro Q2 sales 258 KT vs 431 KT) and DAP (26 KT vs 56 KT), with market share dropping from 34% to 17% in urea and 19% to 13% in DAP. The company attributes declines to planned pricing actions driven by a higher gas cost structure, plus geopolitical supply disruptions. A new CEO (Imran Ahmed) took office May 11, 2026. The PEF project is partially complete. A 4-day unscheduled Base plant outage occurred July 3–10, 2026 (after the reporting period). Full Q2 notes (Annexures A & B) were not provided in the evidence packet.

## What changed

**Performance:** Q2 revenue PKR 33.1 Bn (down 34% YoY); profit PKR 3.8 Bn (down 32%); EPS PKR 2.85 vs 4.17. H1 revenue PKR 70.9 Bn (down 12%); profit PKR 7.1 Bn (down 16%); EPS PKR 5.33 vs 6.34. Dividend cut: Q2'26 PKR 1.75/share vs PKR 4.25/share; YTD PKR 3.75 vs 6.50.

**Volumes:** Urea industry sales up 7% YTD and 18% in Q2, but Engro sales fell from 691 to 537 KT YTD and 431 to 258 KT in Q2. Market share fell from 29% to 21% YTD and 34% to 17% in Q2. DAP industry up 13% YTD but down 30% in Q2; Engro fell from 81 to 67 KT YTD and 56 to 26 KT in Q2; share fell from 18% to 13% YTD.

**Projects:** PEF Phase 1 Scope 1 completed; Scope 2 in progress (expected Q3 2026); Phase 2 expected Q1 2027. Capex surged to PKR 14.8 Bn in H1 2026 vs PKR 3.4 Bn in H1 2025.

**Operations:** Base plant forced outage July 3–10, 2026 (4 days), after the reporting period. Inventory position changed: Engro urea inventory share rose to 74% of total (971 KT) vs 43% (1,307 KT) in 2025.

**Leadership:** Imran Ahmed appointed CEO effective May 11, 2026, for remainder of term. Muhammad Imran Khalil is CFO; Ahsan Zafar Syed is Chairman.

## Decisive evidence

| Claim | Evidence | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Q2 revenue PKR 33.1 Bn, down 34% YoY | "Net sales 33,064,825" vs 50,403,988 | [P061] |
| Q2 profit PKR 3.8 Bn, down 32% | "Profit for the period 3,800,284" vs 5,565,326 | [P061] |
| Q2 EPS PKR 2.85 vs 4.17 | "Earnings per share 2.85 / 4.17" | [P061] |
| Urea market share 17% in Q2 vs 34% | "Market Share (Engro) 17% / 34%" | [P065] |
| DAP market share 13% vs 19% in Q2 | "Market Share 13% / 19%" | [P066] |
| Decline driven by pricing actions, gas cost | "planned pricing actions - necessitated by a comparatively higher gas cost structure" | [P065] |
| SIDC remeasurement gain PKR 1.8 Bn | "Remeasurement gain on provision for SIDC - net 1,802,257" | [P061] |
| New CEO Imran Ahmed from May 11, 2026 | "approved the appointment of Mr. Imran Ahmed as CEO" | [P072] |
| Base plant outage July 3–10, 2026 | "shut down for unscheduled maintenance... 4 days"; "successfully resumed operations" | [P070], [P071] |
| PEF Phase 1 Scope 1 completed | "Scope 1: Completed" | [P069] |
| Debt to capital 56% vs 50% Dec'25 | "Debt to Capital 56% vs 50% on Dec'25" | [P068] |

## Interpretation

The evidence suggests EFERT deliberately sacrificed volume and market share to protect margins amid a higher gas cost structure. Gross margin held at 33% despite revenue decline, supporting this interpretation. The geopolitical shock (Strait of Hormuz disruption, ~30% of global fertilizer flows affected, urea peaking ~$900/t) appears to have driven both input cost pressures and DAP demand destruction (DAP prices PKR 14,000→16,000/bag). The SIDC remeasurement gain of PKR 1.8 Bn is explicitly labeled "one-off" and partially offset other declines. The sharp increase in capex (PKR 14.8 Bn vs 3.4 Bn) aligns with PEF project spending. The post-period outage is not reflected in Q2 results.

## Contradictions and alternative readings

- **Pricing vs demand destruction:** Management attributes urea share loss to "planned pricing actions," but the same briefing notes DAP demand fell due to high prices. It is unclear whether urea share loss was fully voluntary or partly forced by cost competitiveness.
- **Inventory build:** Engro's urea inventory share rose to 74% (971 KT total industry inventory, down from 1,307 KT). This could indicate either deliberate stockpiling for 2H demand recovery (management's claim) or involuntary accumulation from weak sales.
- **SIDC provision:** The balance sheet shows a new non-current SIDC provision of PKR 1.95 Bn while current provision fell from PKR 5.94 Bn to PKR 0.80 Bn, alongside a PKR 1.8 Bn remeasurement gain. The reclassification and gain mechanics are not fully explained in available pages.
- **Cash flow deterioration:** Operating cash flow swung from PKR 928 Mn positive to PKR 21.8 Bn negative (before SIDC/taxes). Management cites "higher working capital requirements," but the scale suggests significant inventory and receivable build-up (stock-in-trade rose from PKR 25.7 Bn to PKR 55.5 Bn; trade debts fell from PKR 16.8 Bn to PKR 3.5 Bn).

## Unknowns

- Full Q2 notes (Annexures A & B) referenced in [P058] were not provided; segment-level Q2 data, detailed volume breakdowns, and gas cost specifics are unavailable.
- The nature and terms of the PKR 39.6 Bn new long-term borrowing (vs PKR 4.0 Bn in H1 2025) are unexplained in available pages.
- The "Gain on subsidy receivable from GoP" (PKR 26.5 Mn H1 2026 vs PKR 192.8 Mn H1 2025) is not explained.
- Whether the July outage affected 2H 2026 production guidance is unknown.
- The earlier CEO disclosure dated March 2, 2026 (referenced in [P072]) is not in the packet.

## Monitoring

| Monitor | New evidence that changes answer | Where it arrives |
|---|---|---|
| EFERT results/reports | Full Q2 notes with segment detail, gas cost, borrowing terms, SIDC mechanics | EFERT Q2 2026 annexures (event-driven) |
| EFERT briefings | 2H 2026 demand recovery evidence; whether market share recovers; PEF completion status | Next corporate briefing (event-driven) |
| EFERT outages | Any production impact from July outage on Q3 volumes; further outages | PSX disclosures (event-driven) |
| EFERT projects | PEF Phase 1 Scope 2 completion (Q3 2026) and Phase 2 (Q1 2027) | PSX disclosures, briefings (event-driven) |
| EFERT leadership | CEO transition effects; any further board changes | PSX disclosures (event-driven) |

sections.title: Fatima company view
sections.question: What does Fatima's latest report show about operating performance, cash generation, balance-sheet movement, capital expenditure and investment exposure, and which portfolio details remain undisclosed?

## Direct answer

Fatima Fertilizer's Q1-2026 report (quarter ended March 31, 2026) shows a sharp deterioration in operating performance: consolidated profit after tax fell 61.4% year-on-year to Rs 3.24 billion, driven by a 9.8% revenue decline, a Rs 3.83 billion revaluation loss on PSX-listed investments held by subsidiary Fatima Capital Limited, and a higher effective tax rate (46.5% vs 38.5%). Cash generation from operations remained positive at Rs 8.58 billion, but net cash used in operating activities was negative (Rs 79.9 million) after finance costs and taxes. The balance sheet shows a major reclassification: current portion of long-term liabilities fell from Rs 37.85 billion to Rs 2.37 billion, while long-term finances secured rose from Rs 2.61 billion to Rs 5.28 billion, reflecting refinancing. Capital expenditure was Rs 2.25 billion (up from Rs 1.46 billion). Investment exposure is significant: short-term investments purchased of Rs 21.33 billion and proceeds of Rs 66.99 billion during the quarter, plus long-term investment purchases of Rs 650 million. Undisclosed portfolio details include the composition of the PSX-listed investments, the nature of short-term investments, and the identity of related parties receiving short-term loans.

## What changed

- **Operating performance**: Revenue down 9.8% to Rs 46.85 billion; gross profit down 11.6% to Rs 18.53 billion; EBITDA down 41.3% to Rs 10.86 billion; PAT down 61.4% to Rs 3.24 billion; EPS down from Rs 3.99 to Rs 1.54 [P084].
- **Cash generation**: Cash generated from operations fell from Rs 9.47 billion to Rs 8.58 billion; net operating cash flow improved from negative Rs 665.6 million to negative Rs 79.9 million [P088].
- **Balance sheet**: Total equity rose from Rs 169.86 billion to Rs 173.10 billion; total assets fell from Rs 360.89 billion to Rs 331.42 billion; current portion of long-term liabilities collapsed from Rs 37.85 billion to Rs 2.37 billion; long-term finances secured more than doubled from Rs 2.61 billion to Rs 5.28 billion [P086].
- **Capital expenditure**: Additions to property, plant and equipment rose from Rs 1.46 billion to Rs 2.25 billion; intangible additions fell from Rs 86.3 million to Rs 3.4 million [P088].
- **Investment exposure**: Revaluation loss of Rs 3.83 billion on PSX-listed investments; KSE-100 fell from 174,054 to 148,743; short-term investment activity was heavy (purchases Rs 21.33 billion, proceeds Rs 66.99 billion); long-term investment purchases rose from Rs 258 million to Rs 650 million [P084][P088].
- **Production**: Combined fertilizer production fell 7% to 673k MT; Sheikhupura plant shut since March due to gas suspension; market share fell from 33.6% to 23.8% [P083][P084].

## Decisive evidence

| Claim | Evidence | Source |
|-------|----------|--------|
| PAT declined 61.4% to Rs 3.24 billion | "consolidated profit after tax to Rs 3.24 billion, compared to Rs 8.37 billion" | [P084] |
| Revaluation loss of Rs 3.83 billion on PSX-listed investments | "revaluation loss of Rs 3.83 billion recognized on PSX-listed investments held by the wholly owned subsidiary, Fatima Capital Limited" | [P084] |
| Cash generated from operations Rs 8.58 billion; net operating cash flow negative Rs 79.9 million | "Cash generated from operations 8,577,709"; "Net cash used in operating activities (79,910)" | [P088] |
| Current portion of long-term liabilities fell from Rs 37.85B to Rs 2.37B; long-term finances rose to Rs 5.28B | "Current portion of long term liabilities 2,371,426" vs "37,850,852"; "Long term finances - secured 5,282,506" vs "2,613,784" | [P086] |
| Capex of Rs 2.25 billion | "Additions in property, plant and equipment (2,246,455)" | [P088] |
| Short-term investments: purchases Rs 21.33B, proceeds Rs 66.99B | "Purchase of short term investments (21,325,948)"; "Proceeds from short term investments 66,992,219" | [P088] |
| Sheikhupura plant shut since March due to gas suspension | "Sheikhupura plant, which has remained shut down since the beginning of March due to suspension of gas supply" | [P083] |

## Interpretation

The Q1-2026 results reflect a company facing simultaneous external shocks: the US-Iran conflict disrupted gas supply (closing the Sheikhupura plant), spiked global fertilizer and raw material prices, and triggered a domestic stock market decline that produced a large unrealized loss on Fatima Capital's equity portfolio. Management frames the revaluation loss as a "partial reversal of substantial unrealized valuation gains recognized in prior periods" with an expectation of reversal upon market recovery [P084].

The balance-sheet movement suggests refinancing activity: the dramatic reduction in current portion of long-term liabilities (from Rs 37.85B to Rs 2.37B) alongside increased long-term finances indicates debt was reclassified or refinanced from short-term to long-term maturity. The cash flow statement confirms this: long-term finance proceeds of Rs 2.71 billion against repayments of Rs 35.58 billion, with short-term finances increasing by Rs 5.68 billion [P088].

The investment exposure is substantial and active. The company's cash and cash equivalents position is negative (Rs 7.72 billion) due to running finance and musharakah of Rs 16.92 billion against cash balances of Rs 9.21 billion [P088]. This suggests the company is running significant short-term borrowings while simultaneously deploying large sums into short-term investments—a strategy that warrants scrutiny given the revaluation losses.

## Contradictions and alternative readings

- **EBITDA vs operating profit**: The Directors' Report shows EBITDA of Rs 10.86 billion, but the income statement shows operating profit (after distribution and admin costs) of Rs 11.28 billion—higher than EBITDA, which is unusual. This may indicate EBITDA is calculated differently (possibly excluding certain items) or there is a presentation inconsistency between the narrative and financial statements [P084][P087].
- **Market share narrative**: The report attributes market share decline primarily to the Nitrogen segment, but the data shows total market volumes grew 3.1% while Fatima's sales fell 27% (from 529k MT to 386k MT). The company says it is "adapting strategies to regain its strong market presence," but no specific plan is disclosed [P083][P084].
- **Tax rate**: The effective tax rate rose from 38.5% to 46.5%, which the report attributes to "higher effective tax rate" without explanation. This is a significant swing that materially reduced profit but is not elaborated [P084].
- **Cash flow classification**: Net cash used in operating activities was negative despite positive cash generation from operations, due to Rs 5.94 billion in taxes paid and Rs 2.62 billion in finance costs. The company's operating cash flow position is weaker than the headline "cash generated from operations" suggests [P088].

## Unknowns

- **Portfolio composition**: The specific holdings within Fatima Capital's PSX-listed investment portfolio are not disclosed—only the aggregate revaluation loss and the KSE-100 index movement are given [P084].
- **Short-term investment nature**: The Rs 21.33 billion purchased and Rs 66.99 billion proceeds from short-term investments are not disaggregated by instrument type (e.g., treasury bills, mutual funds, commercial paper) [P088].
- **Related-party loans**: "Short term loans to related parties - net" of Rs 329.9 million is disclosed in the cash flow statement, but the counterparties and terms are not identified in the provided pages [P088].
- **Long-term advances and deposits**: Net increase of Rs 5.84 billion in long-term advances and deposits is disclosed but not explained in the available pages [P088].
- **Sheikhupura restart timeline**: No date is given for when the Sheikhupura plant might resume operations or when gas supply might be restored [P083].
- **Carveout impact**: The standalone results reflect only the Sadiqabad plant following the Multan plant carveout to Pakarab Fertilizers, but the full financial impact of this restructuring on the consolidated entity is not quantified in the provided pages [P085].

## Monitoring

- **Fatima reports, results and material information (event-driven)**: Any announcement regarding Sheikhupura plant restart, gas supply restoration, or changes to the investment portfolio would change the operating and investment outlook. New evidence would arrive in Fatima's formal disclosures or quarterly reports.
- **Formal reports (quarterly)**: The Q2-2026 report (due for quarter ending June 30, 2026) would show whether the revaluation loss reverses, whether the Sheikhupura plant resumes production, and whether the refinancing trend continues. It would also reveal whether the effective tax rate normalizes and whether market share recovery begins.
monitors: Fatima reports, results and material information: event-driven; formal reports: quarterly

sections.title: Agritech company view
sections.question: What does Agritech's latest report show about operations, profitability, liquidity, financing and preference-share obligations, and how should the FFC relationship be interpreted from the disclosed evidence?
sections.answer:
## Direct answer

Agritech's Q1 2026 report shows deteriorating operations and profitability: urea production fell 18% to 55k tons due to force majeure RLNG curtailment, net sales declined to Rs 7,041m, and the company recorded a Rs 1,020m loss after tax versus Rs 238m loss in Q1 2025. Liquidity remains strained with negative cash and cash equivalents of Rs 404m, though operating cash flow improved to Rs 2,366m. Financing obligations are substantial: preference dividend payable stands at Rs 30,283m, with non-convertible redeemable preference shares of Rs 18,543m. The FFC relationship is best interpreted as a strategic, financially intertwined support arrangement: FFC holds 37.36% equity, provided a Rs 1,318m running finance facility, and converted preference shares into ordinary shares during 2025.

## What changed

- **Operations**: Urea production down 18% (55k vs 67k tons); SSP production up 59% (27k vs 17k tons); SSP sales up 233% (20k vs 6k tons).
- **Profitability**: Operating loss of Rs 367m versus profit of Rs 307m; loss after tax widened to Rs 1,020m from Rs 238m.
- **Liquidity**: Cash and bank balances rose to Rs 486m from Rs 132m; cash and cash equivalents improved to negative Rs 404m from negative Rs 780m at period start.
- **Financing**: Short-term borrowings decreased slightly to Rs 969m; loan from related party (FFC) unchanged at Rs 1,318m.
- **Preference shares**: Preference dividend payable increased to Rs 30,283m from Rs 29,602m; non-convertible preference shares unchanged at Rs 18,543m.
- **FFC relationship**: FFC's equity stake increased to 37.36% during 2025; FFC converted 77,998k convertible preference shares into 91,666k ordinary shares.

## Decisive evidence

| Claim | Evidence | Source |
|-------|----------|--------|
| Urea production fell 18% due to force majeure RLNG curtailment | "produced 55 k tons of urea, compared with 67 k tons in Q1 2025 and the decline of 18% is caused due to the force majeure RLNG supply curtailment" | [P091] |
| Net sales declined to Rs 7,041m from Rs 7,544m | Sales-Net: 7,040,749,024 vs 7,544,111,965 | [P094] |
| Loss after tax of Rs 1,020m vs Rs 238m | Loss after taxation: (1,019,773,694) vs (238,425,170) | [P094] |
| Negative cash and cash equivalents of Rs 404m | "Cash and cash equivalents at end of the period (403,999,208)" | [P095] |
| Operating cash flow improved to Rs 2,366m | "Net cash from operating activities 2,366,479,153" vs 1,003,797,251 | [P095] |
| Preference dividend payable of Rs 30,283m | "Preference dividend payable 30,283,143,235" | [P093] |
| Non-convertible redeemable preference shares of Rs 18,543m | "Non convertible, redeemable preference shares 18,542,697,500" | [P093] |
| FFC holds 37.36% equity stake | "aggregate equity stake increasing to 37.36% at year end" | [P100] |
| FFC provided Rs 1,318m running finance facility | "running finance facility provided to Agritech Limited... maximum amount of loan to AGL outstanding... Rs 1,318,294 thousand" | [P099] |
| FFC converted preference shares to ordinary shares | "Company exercised its option to convert 77,998 thousand listed convertible preference shares of AGL into 91,666 thousand ordinary shares" | [P098] |

## Interpretation

**Operations**: The force majeure gas curtailment is the dominant operational event, directly reducing urea output by 18%. The phosphate/SSP segment partially offsets this with strong growth, but urea remains the core business. The Ghazij/Shawal gas allocation approval is a positive forward-looking development, though implementation remains pending.

**Profitability**: The loss widened significantly. Gross profit halved to Rs 377m, while selling expenses rose 49% to Rs 515m. Finance costs remain heavy at Rs 923m, exceeding gross profit by 2.5 times. The company attributes the decline to gas suspension and inflationary pressures.

**Liquidity**: Despite improved operating cash flow, the company remains in a net debt position on cash equivalents. The Rs 907m capital expenditure in the quarter suggests continued investment, likely related to the gas infrastructure for the Ghazij allocation.

**Financing and preference obligations**: The preference dividend payable of Rs 30.3 billion is the single largest liability, exceeding total equity of Rs 17.9 billion. This represents a structural overhang. The non-convertible preference shares carry KIBOR + 4% dividend, which at current rates is expensive. The company has not redeemed any preference shares during the quarter.

**FFC relationship**: The evidence supports a strategic-support interpretation rather than arm's-length investment. FFC's 37.36% stake, the Rs 1,318m running finance facility at cost-plus-0.10%, and the conversion of preference shares into equity all indicate deep financial integration. FFC's chairman's review explicitly states AGL "remains strategically important for the Group" for "ensuring reliable supply of urea and food security." The loan from related party appears on both companies' books at identical amounts, confirming the facility is active.

## Contradictions and alternative readings

- **Segment reporting discrepancy**: The segment note shows reportable segment liabilities of Rs 83,231m, but after inter-segment eliminations, consolidated liabilities are Rs 76,309m. The elimination increased from Rs 2,637m to Rs 6,922m quarter-over-quarter, suggesting growing inter-segment transactions that are not fully explained.
- **Taxation treatment**: The statement of profit or loss shows "Loss before final & minimum taxes and taxation" of Rs 1,073m, then adds final/minimum tax of Rs 91m, then subtracts taxation credit of Rs 145m. The net effect is a Rs 1,020m loss, but the presentation is unusual and may reflect alternative minimum tax regimes.
- **FFC's investment cost**: FFC's investment in AGL at cost is Rs 7,308m, but FFC also holds 875,948k unlisted preference shares (2024: 190,011k). The increase of 685,937k preference shares during 2025 is not fully explained in the provided evidence—it may relate to the "additional investment of PKR 5.18 billion" mentioned in the chairman's review.
- **Cash flow timing**: Operating cash flow of Rs 2,366m is strong, but the company still ended with negative cash equivalents due to the Rs 907m capex and Rs 1,279m increase in short-term investments. The short-term investment of Rs 10,001m appears to be a deliberate liquidity buffer, possibly earning interest income (Rs 217m received).

## Unknowns

- The status of the Ghazij/Shawal gas allocation implementation timeline.
- Whether preference dividends are being paid or accumulating; the increase of Rs 681m in preference dividend payable suggests accumulation.
- The terms and maturity schedule of the non-convertible preference shares.
- Whether FFC's running finance facility has a defined repayment date.
- The nature of the inter-segment transactions driving the increased elimination amounts.
- Whether the Rs 907m capex relates to gas infrastructure or routine maintenance.

## Monitoring

| Monitor | New evidence that changes answer | Where it arrives |
|---------|----------------------------------|------------------|
| **Agritech financing and filings** | Q2 2026 report showing whether preference dividend payable continues to accumulate, whether the FFC loan is repaid or extended, and whether any preference share redemption occurs | Agritech Q2 2026 interim report (event-driven if material financing events occur) |
| **FFC investment disclosures** | FFC annual report 2026 or interim disclosures showing changes in AGL stake, additional conversions of preference shares, or impairment assessments on the AGL investment | FFC quarterly or annual filings |
| **Gas allocation implementation** | Any announcement that Ghazij/Shawal gas supply has commenced, which would materially improve operations and profitability | Agritech formal reports or regulatory filings |
| **Preference share resolution** | Any restructuring, conversion, or redemption plan for the Rs 30.3 billion preference dividend payable | Agritech formal reports; event-driven if announced |
| **Force majeure resolution** | Confirmation that RLNG supply has normalized and urea production has recovered to prior levels | Agritech Q2 2026 report |
monitors: Agritech financing and filings plus FFC investment disclosures: event-driven; formal reports: quarterly
