sections.question: Compare FFC, EFERT, Fatima and Agritech on operating momentum, exposure to sector drivers, and balance-sheet or capital-allocation risk. Identify provisional conclusions.
sections.answer:
# Comparative Analysis: FFC, EFERT, Fatima, and Agritech

## Operating Momentum

**FFC** shows the strongest operating momentum among the four. H1 2026 revenue rose 28% to PKR 199.6 billion with net profit up 9% to PKR 41.8 billion [P047]. Urea offtake grew 25% to 1,404 KT against production growth of only 3%, implying inventory drawdown or imports [P044][P052]. Market share jumped from 48% to 56% in urea [P052]. However, Q2 standalone profit actually declined year-on-year (PKR 24.37B vs PKR 25.17B) despite higher revenue, indicating Q2 margin compression [P047]. The H1 improvement is driven primarily by Q1 performance.

**EFERT** is in deliberate retreat. Q2 2026 revenue fell 34% YoY, profit fell 32%, and EPS dropped from PKR 4.17 to PKR 2.85 [P061]. Urea market share collapsed from 34% to 17% in Q2; DAP share fell from 19% to 13% [P065][P066]. Management attributes this to "planned pricing actions" necessitated by a higher gas cost structure [P065]. Gross margin held at 33%, supporting the interpretation that EFERT sacrificed volume to protect margins. A 4-day unscheduled Base plant outage occurred July 3–10, 2026, after the reporting period [P070][P071].

**Fatima** shows sharp deterioration. Q1 2026 consolidated PAT fell 61.4% to Rs 3.24 billion [P084]. Revenue declined 9.8%, and the Sheikhupura plant has been shut since March due to gas suspension [P083]. Market share fell from 33.6% to 23.8% [P084]. A Rs 3.83 billion revaluation loss on PSX-listed investments held by subsidiary Fatima Capital Limited compounded operating weakness [P084]. The effective tax rate rose from 38.5% to 46.5% without explanation [P084].

**Agritech** is the weakest operator. Q1 2026 urea production fell 18% to 55k tons due to force majeure RLNG curtailment [P091]. Loss after tax widened to Rs 1,020m from Rs 238m [P094]. SSP production rose 59% and sales rose 233%, partially offsetting urea weakness [P091]. Operating cash flow improved to Rs 2,366m, but the company remains in negative cash and cash equivalents of Rs 404m [P095].

**Momentum ranking: FFC > EFERT > Fatima > Agritech**, though FFC's Q2 weakness and EFERT's deliberate strategy complicate simple ordering.

## Exposure to Sector Drivers

**Gas supply and pricing** is the dominant sector driver. FFC's DAP production fell 6% due to gas curtailment and phosphoric acid shortage [P044]. EFERT's higher gas cost structure drove its pricing strategy [P065]. Fatima's Sheikhupura plant is shut due to gas suspension from the US-Iran conflict [P083]. Agritech's urea production fell 18% due to force majeure RLNG curtailment [P091]. All four are exposed, but Fatima and Agritech face the most acute operational disruption.

**Geopolitical shocks** hit all players. The Strait of Hormuz disruption affected ~30% of global fertilizer flows, with urea peaking around $900/t [P065]. This drove input costs up and DAP demand destruction (prices rose from PKR 14,000 to 16,000/bag) [P065]. FFC's flat other income despite larger investment balances may reflect lower yields in this environment [P047].

**Market share dynamics** differentiate the companies. FFC gained share (48% to 56% urea) [P052]. EFERT lost share deliberately (34% to 17% in Q2) [P065]. Fatima lost share (33.6% to 23.8%) [P084]. Agritech's share position is not directly quantified but production declines imply pressure.

**Inventory dynamics** are mixed. FFC's stock-in-trade rose 68% to PKR 64.4B [P046]. EFERT's stock-in-trade rose from PKR 25.7B to PKR 55.5B, with industry urea inventory falling from 1,307 KT to 971 KT while Engro's share rose to 74% [P068]. This could indicate deliberate stockpiling or involuntary accumulation.

**Investment portfolio exposure** is significant for FFC and Fatima. FFC holds PKR 284.2 billion in total investments (PKR 174.4 billion short-term) [P056]. Fatima's subsidiary Fatima Capital holds PSX-listed investments that produced a Rs 3.83 billion revaluation loss as the KSE-100 fell from 174,054 to 148,743 [P084].

## Balance-Sheet and Capital-Allocation Risk

**FFC** is increasing leverage and investment simultaneously. Long-term borrowings rose 44% to PKR 72.4B in H1 2026 [P046], and debt-to-equity shifted from 27:73 to 32:68 [P056]. The PKR 30.6B PIA Equity investment and advance is the largest single investing outflow [P048]. Fixed capex surged 3.3x to PKR 23.6B [P048]. The AGL exposure is modest—PKR 7.31B equity at cost plus PKR 1.32B loan against PKR 284.2B total investments [P097][P099]. The FPCL acquisition via share issuance (15.9M FFC shares for 214.7M FPCL shares) requires regulatory approvals not yet obtained [P098]. GIDC payable of PKR 84.98B remains contested with a stay in place [P077].

**EFERT** shows deteriorating cash flow and rising leverage. Operating cash flow swung from PKR 928M positive to PKR 21.8B negative [P068]. Debt to capital rose from 50% to 56% [P068]. A PKR 39.6B new long-term borrowing (vs PKR 4.0B in H1 2025) is unexplained in available pages [P068]. Capex surged to PKR 14.8B in H1 2026 vs PKR 3.4B, aligned with PEF project spending [P069]. The SIDC remeasurement gain of PKR 1.8B is explicitly one-off [P061].

**Fatima** shows refinancing activity and heavy investment churn. Current portion of long-term liabilities collapsed from Rs 37.85B to Rs 2.37B while long-term finances rose to Rs 5.28B, indicating debt reclassification or refinancing [P086]. Short-term investment activity was heavy: purchases of Rs 21.33B and proceeds of Rs 66.99B during the quarter [P088]. Cash and cash equivalents are negative (Rs 7.72B) due to running finance and musharakah of Rs 16.92B against cash of Rs 9.21B [P088]. The company is running significant short-term borrowings while deploying large sums into short-term investments.

**Agritech** carries structural financing risk. Preference dividend payable stands at Rs 30,283m, exceeding total equity of Rs 17.9B [P093]. Non-convertible redeemable preference shares of Rs 18,543m carry KIBOR + 4% dividends [P093][P098]. The preference dividend payable increased by Rs 681m during the quarter, suggesting accumulation rather than payment [P093]. Finance costs of Rs 923m exceed gross profit of Rs 377m by 2.5 times [P094]. The FFC relationship provides support—37.36% equity, Rs 1,318m running finance at cost-plus-0.10%, and preference share conversions—but this is a strategic support arrangement, not an arm's-length investment [P098][P099][P100].

**Risk ranking: Agritech > Fatima > EFERT > FFC**, though FFC's rising leverage and PIA Equity investment warrant monitoring.

## Provisional Conclusions

1. **FFC is the relative winner on operating momentum** but faces rising leverage, a large unproven PIA Equity investment, and Q2 margin compression that may signal a turning point. The flat other income despite larger investment balances is a yellow flag.

2. **EFERT's strategy is a deliberate margin-protection play** that sacrifices market share. The strategy is coherent if gas cost disadvantages persist, but the negative operating cash flow and unexplained PKR 39.6B borrowing raise questions about sustainability.

3. **Fatima faces compounding external shocks**—gas disruption, market decline, and tax rate increase—with the investment portfolio adding volatility. The refinancing activity suggests liability management, but the negative cash position and heavy short-term investment churn warrant scrutiny.

4. **Agritech is a distressed entity dependent on FFC support.** The preference dividend overhang exceeds equity, and the company cannot service its obligations from operations. The Ghazij/Shawal gas allocation is the key potential catalyst but implementation remains pending.

## Decision Implication

For an investor or lender, FFC offers the strongest operating fundamentals but requires monitoring of the PIA Equity investment and Q2 margin trend. EFERT is a bet on gas cost normalization and market share recovery. Fatima is exposed to external shocks with portfolio volatility. Agritech is not investable without FFC support and a resolution of the preference share overhang.

## Unresolved Evidence Gaps

1. **FFC Q2 full report** (expected via PUCARS) would resolve other income composition, PIA Equity details, segment costs, and borrowing terms [P045].

2. **EFERT Q2 annexures** (Annexures A & B referenced in [P058]) would provide segment data, gas cost specifics, and the PKR 39.6B borrowing terms.

3. **Fatima's investment portfolio composition** is undisclosed—only aggregate revaluation loss and index movement are given [P084].

4. **Agritech's preference share resolution**—whether dividends are accumulating and whether any redemption or restructuring is planned—remains unknown [P093].

5. **FPCL regulatory approvals** for FFC's share issuance are pending [P098].

6. **GIDC litigation outcome** for FFC remains uncertain despite the Supreme Court upholding the Act [P077].

7. **Fatima's Sheikhupura restart timeline** is undisclosed [P083].

8. **Agritech's Ghazij/Shawal gas allocation implementation** timeline is unknown [P091].

# Pakistan Fertilizer Sector: Strongest Current Thesis, Evidence, and Falsification Conditions

## Strongest Current Sector Thesis

**The sector is bifurcating: urea is in surplus with demand recovering sharply, while DAP is structurally tight and import-dependent, creating divergent margin and risk profiles across companies based on gas cost structures and product mix.**

The strongest formulation combines three evidence-backed pillars:

**Pillar 1 — Urea oversupply with demand recovery.** Kharif 2026 urea availability is projected at 4,083 thousand tonnes against demand of 3,498 thousand tonnes, leaving 574 thousand tonnes closing stock—an excess of 274 thousand tonnes [P005]. April 2026 actuals confirm the surplus: production (476 kt) exceeded offtake (463 kt), with inventory flat at 805 kt [P004]. Urea offtake surged 84.9% year-on-year [P001], and FY2025-26 (Jul-Apr) urea offtake is running 21.6% above prior year [P009].

**Pillar 2 — DAP tightness approaching zero buffer.** Kharif 2026 DAP availability is 711 thousand tonnes against demand of 695 thousand tonnes, leaving only 17 thousand tonnes closing stock [P005]. This depends on 55 thousand tonnes of imports arriving June-July [P005], uninterrupted gas supply [P002], and offtake following the five-year average. The March 2026 review projected a *negative* closing stock of -31 thousand tonnes, corrected only by adding imports in April [P017][P005].

**Pillar 3 — Gas cost structure is the decisive competitive variable.** Feed gas on SNGPL/SSGC systems is Rs 1,597/MMBTU versus Rs 580/MMBTU on the Mari system [P028]. RLNG-dependent plants face US$23.70/MMBTU [P039]. EFERT explicitly attributes its urea market share collapse (34% to 17% in Q2) to "planned pricing actions—necessitated by a comparatively higher gas cost structure" [P065]. FFC's urea share rose from 48% to 56% [P052].

## Supporting Evidence

**Demand recovery is real but uneven.** Total nutrient offtake rose 44.1% year-on-year in April 2026; nitrogen up 62%, potash up 55.1%, phosphate down 5% [P001][P003]. NFDC projects 2025-26 urea offtake +17.4% but DAP -2.7% [P023]. The April urea surge follows a depressed base (April 2025 was -24% YoY) [P001][P003].

**Price transmission is occurring.** All domestic prices rose in April 2026 versus March: urea +1.8%, DAP +2.9%, SSP +3.8%, SOP +6.0% [P001][P006]. DAP retail reached Rs 14,675/bag, up 18.7% year-on-year [P006]. International urea (Middle East) rose from US$745-780 to US$830-900 through April; DAP (Morocco) from US$760-845 to US$821-950 [P007].

**Company results confirm divergence.** FFC H1'26 revenue +28%, net profit +9% [P054]. EFERT Q2'26 revenue -34%, profit -32% [P067]. Fatima Q1'26 PAT -61.4% with Sheikhupura plant shut since March due to gas suspension [P083][P084]. Agritech Q1'26 loss widened to Rs 1,020m from Rs 238m on force majeure RLNG curtailment [P091][P094].

**Subsidy withdrawal is shifting costs.** Feed gas subsidy fell from Rs 121.20 billion to Rs 84.49 billion (-30.3%), with SNGPL and SSGC subsidies eliminated entirely [P028].

## Contradicting Evidence

**"Favorable farmer economics" versus deteriorating exchange ratios.** Engro attributes urea demand growth to "favorable farmer economics" [P065], but NFDC data shows crop-to-fertilizer exchange ratios worsened sharply in 2024-25: wheat required 56.6% more kg to buy 1 kg of N; paddy required ~71% more [P026]. Wheat market prices fell from Rs 3,369 to Rs 2,217 per 40 kg while urea prices rose [P025]. The April 2026 surge may reflect restocking or pre-buying rather than sustained affordability.

**DAP demand data conflict.** NFDC reports DAP offtake -10.8% in April 2026 [P001], but Engro reports industry DAP sales +13% YTD [P066]. This may reflect Q1 pre-buying ahead of price increases, with Q2 sales down 30% [P066].

**FFC's Q2 weakness contradicts H1 strength.** FFC's H1 improvement is driven primarily by Q1; Q2 standalone profit actually declined year-on-year (PKR 24.37B vs PKR 25.17B) despite higher revenue [P047]. FFC's stock-in-trade rose 68% to PKR 64.4B, with "higher DAP inventory" cited [P056]—this could be speculative stocking, not operational efficiency.

**EFERT's margin maintenance may be one-off.** EFERT held gross margin at 33% despite revenue decline [P068], but this may reflect a SIDC provision remeasurement gain explicitly described as one-off [P061].

**Policy priority versus discretionary allocation.** The 2005 Natural Gas Allocation Policy gives fertilizer second priority on system gas and first on independent networks [P043], but allocation volumes are set by the Federal Government "keeping in view the domestic needs and gas supply position" [P041]—discretion that could override stated priority.

## Falsification Conditions

**The urea surplus thesis is falsified if:** (a) May 2026 urea offtake falls well below the 500 kt projection [P005], indicating the April surge was a base-effect artifact; (b) any plant shutdown or gas curtailment reduces production below the "all plants operational" assumption [P005]; (c) Kharif closing stock projections are revised downward from 574 kt [P005].

**The DAP tightness thesis is falsified if:** (a) The 55 kt of scheduled DAP imports arrive early or in larger volumes [P005]; (b) DAP offtake falls below the 695 kt projection due to price-driven demand destruction [P005]; (c) domestic DAP production increases beyond current levels.

**The gas-cost competitive thesis is falsified if:** (a) SNGPL/SSGC feed gas prices fall toward Mari-system levels (Rs 580/MMBTU) [P028]; (b) RLNG prices decline substantially from US$23.70/MMBTU [P039]; (c) EFERT's market share recovers without gas cost normalization, suggesting the decline was strategic rather than cost-forced.

**The demand recovery thesis is falsified if:** (a) Urea offtake reverts to single-digit growth in May-June 2026; (b) institutional agricultural credit expansion cited by Engro [P064] fails to materialize; (c) weather conditions deteriorate, invalidating the "favorable weather" assumption [P064].

## Next Publications and Events That Can Change Each Conclusion

**Urea surplus conclusion:** The **NFDC May 2026 monthly review** will show whether May urea offtake tracked the 500 kt projection [P005]. If offtake falls well below, the surplus narrative strengthens; if it exceeds, the surplus narrows. Any revision to Kharif closing stock estimates would directly change the balance.

**DAP tightness conclusion:** The **NFDC June 2026 monthly review** will reveal whether the 35 kt of June DAP imports materialized [P005]. If imports slip, the projected 17 kt closing stock could turn negative, intensifying tightness. Gas supply or plant shutdown announcements would also change this conclusion.

**Gas-cost competitive thesis:** **OGRA monthly price notifications** will show whether SNGPL/SSGC feed gas prices changed from Rs 1,597/MMBTU or Mari-system prices from Rs 580/MMBTU [P028]. A sustained RLNG price decline would improve Agritech and Fatimafert economics [P039].

**Demand recovery thesis:** **NFDC monthly reviews for May-June 2026** will confirm whether urea offtake sustains above +50% YoY or reverts to single digits. **Issuer Q3 2026 result briefings** will reveal whether Engro's inventory drawdown and market share recovery materialize [P065], and whether FFC's share gains persist [P052].

**Company-level conclusions:** **FFC Q2 full report** (via PUCARS) would resolve other income composition, PIA Equity details, and borrowing terms [P045]. **EFERT Q2 annexures** would provide segment data and the unexplained PKR 39.6B borrowing terms [P058][P068]. **Fatima's Sheikhupura restart timeline** is undisclosed [P083]. **Agritech's Ghazij/Shawal gas allocation implementation** timeline is unknown [P091].

## Decision Implication

For an investor or lender, the sector thesis supports **overweight FFC relative to peers** on operating momentum and market share gains [P052][P054], but requires monitoring of rising leverage (debt-to-equity shifted from 27:73 to 32:68) [P056] and the unproven PIA Equity investment [P048]. **EFERT is a bet on gas cost normalization**—the strategy is coherent if cost disadvantages persist, but negative operating cash flow (PKR 21.8B) and rising debt-to-capital (56%) raise sustainability questions [P068]. **Fatima and Agritech face acute operational disruption**—Fatima's Sheikhupura plant is shut [P083], and Agritech's preference dividend payable (Rs 30,283m) exceeds total equity (Rs 17.9B) [P093]. The DAP tightness supports **positive exposure to DAP inventory holders**—FFC's stock-in-trade rose to PKR 64.4B [P056]—but import-dependent players face margin compression as international prices rise [P007].

## Unresolved Evidence Gaps

1. **Current gas allocation volumes**: No evidence of 2025-26 or 2026-27 allocation letters to individual fertilizer plants.
2. **Post-January 2025 feed gas prices**: Whether SNGPL/SSGC or Mari-system prices changed after the last data point [P028].
3. **Company-level gas costs**: Regulated prices are provided [P028], but actual contracted prices and volumes per company for 2026 are not.
4. **Importer margins**: No data on importers' cost structures or realized margins for DAP.
5. **Urea offtake surge drivers**: No explanation for the 84.9% increase [P001]—restocking, pre-buying, or genuine demand.
6. **Credit impact**: Engro cites "projected increase in institutional agricultural credit" [P064], but no disbursement data is provided.
7. **EFERT's PKR 39.6B new long-term borrowing**: Unexplained in available pages [P068].
8. **Fatima's investment portfolio composition**: Only aggregate revaluation loss is given [P084].
9. **Agritech's preference share resolution**: Whether dividends are accumulating and whether redemption or restructuring is planned [P093].
10. **Current subsidy status**: Data covers 2024-25 [P028]; whether the Rs 84.49 billion level persists into 2025-26 or 2026-27 is unknown.

# Executive Summary: Pakistan Fertilizer Sector — Kharif 2026

## What Is Happening Now

Pakistan's fertilizer market entered Kharif 2026 with a **comfortable urea surplus but a structurally tight DAP position**. As of April 2026, urea closing inventory was 805 thousand tonnes against monthly offtake of 463 thousand tonnes—roughly 1.7 months of cover. DAP closing inventory was 203 thousand tonnes against monthly offtake of 85 thousand tonnes—about 2.4 months of cover, but projected to fall to just 17 thousand tonnes by September 2026 [P004][P005].

**Urea offtake surged 84.9% year-on-year** in April 2026 to 463 thousand tonnes, while DAP offtake fell 10.8% to 85 thousand tonnes [P001][P003]. All domestic fertilizer prices rose month-on-month in April 2026—urea +1.8%, DAP +2.9%, SSP +3.8%, SOP +6.0% [P001][P006]. DAP retail reached Rs 14,675 per bag, up 18.7% year-on-year [P006].

**Company performance is sharply divergent.** FFC's H1 2026 revenue rose 28% to PKR 199.6 billion with net profit up 9%, and urea market share jumped from 48% to 56% [P047][P052]. EFERT's Q2 2026 revenue fell 34% and profit fell 32%, with urea market share collapsing from 34% to 17%—attributed to "planned pricing actions—necessitated by a comparatively higher gas cost structure" [P061][P065]. Fatima's Q1 2026 profit fell 61.4% with its Sheikhupura plant shut since March due to gas suspension [P083][P084]. Agritech's Q1 loss widened to Rs 1,020 million on force majeure RLNG curtailment [P091][P094].

## Variables Most Likely to Change the View

**1. Gas supply and pricing.** Feed gas on SNGPL/SSGC systems is Rs 1,597/MMBTU versus Rs 580/MMBTU on the Mari system; RLNG-dependent plants face US$23.70/MMBTU [P028][P039]. The Kharif 2026 outlook assumes "all plants will remain operational" [P005]. Any curtailment or price change directly alters competitive positions.

**2. DAP import timing.** Only 55 thousand tonnes of DAP imports are scheduled for June-July 2026 [P005]. The March review projected a *negative* closing stock of -31 thousand tonnes, corrected only by adding imports in April [P017][P005]. If imports slip, the projected 17 thousand tonne closing stock could turn negative.

**3. Urea demand sustainability.** April's 84.9% offtake surge follows a depressed base (April 2025 was -24% YoY) [P001][P003]. Whether this reflects genuine farmer purchasing power or one-time restocking is unverified.

**Established facts:** Urea surplus and DAP tightness projections [P005]; April 2026 offtake and production figures [P001][P003]; price increases across products [P006]; gas price differentials [P028]; company financial results [P047][P061][P084][P094]; EFERT's explicit attribution of share loss to gas cost structure [P065]; subsidy reduction [P028].

**Inference:** That EFERT's margin preservation (33% gross margin) is sustainable—this may reflect a one-off SIDC provision remeasurement gain [P061][P068]. That FFC's DAP inventory build (stock-in-trade up 68% to PKR 64.4 billion) represents speculative stocking rather than operational efficiency [P046][P056]. That the April urea surge reflects sustained demand recovery—contradicted by NFDC data showing crop-to-fertilizer exchange ratios worsened 56-71% in 2024-25 [P026].

**EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

Fertilizer is the key crop production input. Its contribution towards crop productivity enhancement is from 30 to 50 per cent. An increase in price of fertilizer by Rs. 100 per 50 kg bag puts an additional financial burden of Rs. 20 billion per annum on farming community. Therefore, monitoring of fertilizer supply / demand and prices situation has gained immense importance with respect to policy formulation and is one of the core activities of National Fertilizer Development Centre (NFDC). Highlights of fiscal year 2024-25, Kharif 2024 and Rabi 2024-25 with regard to fertilizer sector are given below.

**Fertilizer Supply**

Overall fertilizer availability during 2024-25 was 5,333 thousand nutrient tonnes, which witnessed an increase of 0.85 per cent over last fiscal year 2023-24. Total availability of nitrogen, phosphate and potash was 4,155, 1,121 and 57 thousand nutrient tonnes, respectively. Product-wise availability was; urea 7,210, DAP 1,856 and Nitrophos 1,114 thousand product tonnes. About 90.6 per cent of the country’s requirement during 2024-25 was met through domestic production. The deficit of 9.4 per cent between production and offtake was met through imports and carry over inventory.

**Domestic Production**

Total domestic production of all fertilizer products during 2024-25 was 9,505 thousand tonnes compared to 9,362 thousand tonnes during 2023-24, showing an increase of 1.5 per cent. This was mainly due to enhancement in production of urea from FFC (Port Qasim) plant as a result of improved gas availability. Urea production during 2024-25 was 6,780 thousand tonnes (6,591 thousand tonnes in 2023-24) followed by NP 865, CAN 855, DAP 844, SSP 80, NPK of various grades 41 and SOP 40 thousand tonnes.

The production, in nutrient terms, increased from 4,240 thousand tonnes during 2023-24 to 4,322 thousand tonnes during 2024-25; showing an increase of 1.9 per cent. Nitrogen production was 3,694 thousand tonnes (85.5 per cent share in total nutrients production) and recorded an increase of 1.9 per cent while phosphate production was 601 thousand tonnes (13.9 per cent share in total nutrients production), which remained at previous year level. Potash production (in NPKs and SOP) was 27 thousand tonnes (0.6 per cent share in total nutrients production) and recorded an increase of 74.2 per cent, over 2023-24.

### Imports

### Offtake

Offtake of all nutrients during 2024-25 was 4,351 thousand tonnes as compared to 4,816 thousand tonnes in 2023-24, representing a decrease of 9.7 per cent. Out of this, nitrogen, phosphate and potash were 3,387, 919 and 44.5 thousand tonnes, respectively. A decrease of 10.3 per cent was observed in nitrogen, 7.6 per cent in phosphate and 1.1 per cent in potash during 2024-25 as compared to 2023-24. Fertilizer offtake declined during 2024-25 as a result of poor farm economics due to low market prices of wheat. Urea offtake registered a decrease of 10.5 per cent from 6,579 thousand tonnes in 2023-24 to 5,890 thousand tonnes in 2024-25. The DAP offtake also decreased from 1,615 thousand tonnes in 2023-24 to 1,542 thousand tonnes in 2024-25; representing a decline of 4.5 per cent. The offtake of other products during 2024-25 was: NP 854, CAN 711, SSP 71, AS 69, SOP 56, NPK's 43, MOP 15 and MAP 1 thousand tonnes.

### Nutrients Use Ratio

Balanced nutrient's use is the key to determine yield and quality of crops. Nitrogen to phosphate use ratio was 3.68:1 during 2024-25 against recommended ratio of 2:1. Potash use far less than requirement is impacting negatively crops' productivity. Provincial Agriculture departments will have to adopt the implementable strategies for promoting use of potash keeping in view the small farmers' constraints and high cost of potassic fertilizers.

### Province-wise Offtake/Shares

Punjab's share in overall nutrient offtake during 2024-25 was 69.4 per cent, Sindh 23.1 per cent, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 4.2 per cent and Balochistan 3.1 per cent. The overall provincial share remained more or less the same as was witnessed during the preceding years.

## Global Fertilizer Situation

The world fertilizer consumption data depicts that fertilizer consumption was around 
206 million nutrient tonnes in fertilizer year 2024-25 which was 4.4 per cent higher compared 
with previous year. Major increase (9.2 %) was observed in potash followed by nitrogen (3.6 
%) and phosphate (2.5 %). The sustained growth in global N use during 2023-24 and 2024-25 
was primarily driven by improved affordability and reinforced by food security policies in 
several of the world's most populous countries such as China and India.

## Economics of Fertilizer Use

The benefit cost ratio of farmer changes with passage of time due to variation in prices of 
fertilizers and major crops. Average price of urea during Kharif 2024 increased by 
Rs. 1,428 while that of DAP by Rs. 1,247 per 50 kg bag over Kharif 2023. 
During Rabi 2024-25, an increase of Rs. 131 per 50 kg bag in price of urea was witnessed 
over Rabi 2023-24. In contrast, price of DAP decreased by Rs. 717 per 50 kg bag. Market 
price of sugarcane increased by Rs. 8 per 40 kg while market price of wheat and seed cotton 
decreased by Rs. 1152 and Rs. 11 per 40 kg during 2024-25 compared with 2023-24. 
Similarly, prices of IRRI and Basmati declined by Rs. 440 per 40 kg bag and Rs. 762 per 40 
kg bag, respectively. Hence both Urea (nitrogen) and DAP (phosphorus) fertilizer remained 
costlier for all crops during 2024-25 compared with the previous year. It was due to increase 
in prices of fertilizer and decline in commodity prices.

## Demand Forecast: Outlook 2025-26

Recovery in fertilizer offtake as a result of soaring prices of wheat is expected during 
2025-26. As a result, fertilizer demand is projected to increase by 8.7 per cent in nutrient

terms during 2025-26. In product terms, offtake of urea is estimated to increase by 17.4 per cent. However, DAP offtake is expected to decrease slightly by 2.7 per cent mainly due its high prices.

## Policy Issues

There is inequality in price of feedstock gas for fertilizer plants receiving gas from different distribution companies although the price of finished product is more or less the same. Plants receiving gas from Mari Energies are enjoying concessional price of feedstock gas (Rs. 580 per MMBTU).

Imposition of 5% GST on DAP imports has disturbed the level playing field for private importers as compared to local manufacturer which has resulted in higher DAP prices and its less use.

There is need to have a new fertilizer policy keeping in view the future needs of the crops, depleting reserves of natural resources / raw materials globally and greenhouse gas emissions in the field. Incentives to fertilizer industry should be linked to production of efficient fertilizer products.

To mitigate the impact of high DAP prices, awareness regarding use of other cheaper sources of phosphate i.e. Triple Super Phosphate (TSP), Nitrophos (NP) and Single Super Phosphate (SSP) needs to be created among farming community by Provincial Agriculture Departments.

1. INTRODUCTION

Pakistan has limited natural gas deposits. At present, recoverable natural gas reserves in Pakistan are 32 Trillion Cubic Feet (TCF) and Reserve to Production (R/P) ratio based on current production of 3.7 Billion Cubic Feet per Day (BCFD) is 23 years. One of the significant developments in local gas market is the increase of natural gas share in primary energy supply mix from about 40% in 1999-2000 to over 52% in 2004-05 in about five years. If the demand/supply trend of past five years is maintained, the R/P ratio reduces significantly necessitating urgent need to increase natural gas supply. The Government of Pakistan has accordingly placed the highest priority to (a) enhance indigenous natural gas supplies through intensified exploration efforts, and (b) import natural gas through pipeline from neighbouring countries as well as LNG.

While the Federal Government is making concerted efforts to enhance natural gas supplies to meet growing demand, it is extremely important to establish a natural gas allocation and management plan to promote efficacious utilization of precious depleting natural resource particularly given the dominant role of natural gas in domestic energy landscape. Therefore, the Federal Government has set out these policy guidelines for the purpose in the paragraphs that follow.

# Q2 2026 – Agricultural Landscape

### 1. Farmer Economics
Farmer economics were broadly positive, Punjab's official wheat support price of PKR 3,500/maund and open market prices of PKR 3,700–4,650 per 40 kg improved returns for wheat growers; however, DAP prices surging from PKR 14,000 to PKR 16,000/bag significantly compressed demand and impacted farmer affordability, particularly for smallholder farmers.

Improved rice prices (IRRI-6: PKR 3,000-3,200/maund; Long Grain: PKR 4,000-4,400/maund), is expected to enhance farmer liquidity and support fertilizer consumption, provided weather conditions remain favourable.

### 2. Water Avails
Stable water supply and favourable crop conditions supported the season with no major climate-related disruptions and encouraging crop prospects. Looking ahead, satisfactory water availability in reservoirs and canal systems is supporting ongoing Kharif sowing activity, with favourable crop outlooks expected to sustain healthy fertilizer demand.

### 3. Input Costs
Farm input costs rose in Q2 2026, primarily driven by fuel price escalation — while DAP prices spiked sharply on global supply disruptions.

While geopolitical uncertainty and its impact on input costs remains a risk, projected increase in institutional agricultural credit alongside healthy water availability and strong wheat returns, should help sustain farmer confidence and cushion elevated input costs.

# Directors' Report

To the Shareholders for the First Quarter ended March 31, 2026

On behalf of the Board of Directors of Fatima Fertilizer Company Limited (the Company), we are pleased to present a brief overview of the Company's performance and condensed interim consolidated and standalone financial statements for the first quarter of the year 2026.

## The Economy

The escalation of the US-Iran conflict has triggered a significant negative supply shock, with the World Bank warning of a "cascading impact" that could reduce emerging market growth to 2.6%–3.65% in 2026. The conflict has driven a sharp increase in global oil prices, fueling inflationary pressures and heightening risks to food security. At the same time, debt-constrained developing economies face limited fiscal space to absorb these shocks. The economic fallout could intensify further in the event of a breakdown in ceasefire arrangements and a broader regional escalation.

Against this backdrop, the near-term outlook for Pakistan remains cautiously optimistic, albeit with rising downside risks. The rebuilding of foreign exchange reserves over the past year provides a degree of resilience against external shocks. Additionally, Pakistan's evolving role as a peace facilitator would help secure continued backing from key bilateral partners and strengthen its engagement with global financial institutions.

However, the economy remains highly susceptible to elevated global energy prices, posing a significant risk to external stability, particularly if these pressures strain foreign exchange reserves. Structural challenges, including high public debt, energy shortages, and the risk of growth moderation due to rising fuel costs, continue to weigh on the outlook. In the near term, Pakistan's economic trajectory is being shaped increasingly by geopolitics as by domestic policy choices.

## Fertilizer Market

### International

Global fertilizer markets experienced a pronounced uptrend in Q1 2026, particularly toward the latter part of the quarter due to escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Disruptions to the flow of key raw materials, including phosphates, ammonia, and Sulphur, constrained global availability and intensified price volatility.

# Local

In Q1-2026 supply security and price expectations shaped fertilizer demand patterns instead of underlying agronomic fundamentals. Anticipation of further price increases and potential supply disruptions due to US-Iran conflict led to substantial increase in phosphate offtake. As a result, despite a 9.0% decline in nitrogenous fertilizer offtake, total market volumes increased by 3.1% to 1,626k MT, compared to 1,577k MT in the corresponding period last year.

DAP offtake surged by 84.1% to 276k MT, exceeding its three-year historical average by 19.6%, while Nitrophos increased by 29.6% to 169k MT, 6.8% above its three-year average. The elevated offtake levels suggest demand pull-forward rather than purely consumption-driven growth, indicating potential normalization in subsequent quarters.

Nitrogen demand weakened due to both structural and transient factors. Urea offtake declined by 5.6% year-on-year to 1,038k MT, reflecting carryover inventory effects and subdued farm economics. Gas supply disruptions resulted in the shutdown of two RLNG-based plants, tightening supply and limiting market throughput. Calcium Ammonium Nitrate (CAN) exhibited a sharper contraction of 29.9%, indicating greater elasticity to price and substitution dynamics within the nitrogen segment.

# Directors' Review Report

The Board of Directors hereby presents its review report along with the unaudited condensed interim financial statements for the quarter ended March 31, 2026.

**Overview of Fertilizer Industry:**

During the first quarter of 2026, Pakistan's urea industry remained broadly stable, though operating conditions were shaped by planned annual turnaround activities at major plants. National urea production recorded a marginal decline of 0.6% to 1,560 k tons, compared with 1,568 k tons in the corresponding period of 2025. Urea offtakes, however, eased by 5.6% to 1,038 k tons from 1,100 k tons last year, reflecting utilization of carry over channel stock from last year and prevailing less favourable wheat farm economics.

Within this environment, the Company produced 55 k tons of urea, compared with 67 k tons in Q1 2025 and the decline of 18% is caused due to the force majeure RLNG supply curtailment, arising from the ongoing Middle East conflict. Notwithstanding these disruptions, the Company recorded urea sales of 70 k tons during the quarter, as against 89 k tons in the corresponding period last year.

The phosphate segment, by contrast, exhibited strong momentum. Phosphate offtakes increased sharply by 79% to 178 k tons of P2O5 nutrients, compared with 100 k tons in the same period last year. Phosphatic fertilizer production rose modestly by 3% to 130 k tons of P2O5 nutrients, while imports expanded significantly by 84% to 59 k tons of P2O5 nutrients, versus 32 k tons in Q1 2025. International DAP prices remained on a firm upward trajectory throughout the quarter, rising from USD 672 per ton CFR Karachi at the beginning of the year to USD 805 per ton CFR Karachi by the close of the period. The sharp escalation witnessed in March was driven primarily by the Middle East conflict causing supply chain disruption and production curtailment, which materially affected international pricing dynamics.

As a major player in the SSP segment, the Company delivered a particularly strong performance in this category. SSP production increased to 27 k tons during the quarter, compared with 17 k tons in Q1 2025, while sales rose to 20 k tons from 6 k tons in the corresponding period last year, reflecting a meaningful improvement in both production scale and market absorption.

Dear Shareholders,

The year 2025 represents another year of solid performance wherein the Group continued to build long-term value for its stakeholders.

The Group's financial results for 2025 comprise of full year operations of ex-FFBL along with its subsidiaries including FFBL Power Company Limited (FPCL) and Fauji Foods Limited (FFL) subsequent to merger with and into FFC, compared to second half operations only during 2024.

Food business delivered a strong turnaround during the year. FFL contributed its highest-ever profit after tax of PKR 1.3 billion to Group profitability, while Fauji Fresh n Freeze (FFF) also registered its first ever profitability of PKR 201 million during 2025.

The wind energy portfolio, comprising FFC Energy Limited (FFCEL), Foundation Wind Energy -I Limited (FWEL-I) and Foundation Wind Energy -II Limited (FWEL-II), remained important contributors to the power sector of the country during the year. All three projects maintained availability factors above benchmark levels and collectively supplied 261 GWh of electricity to National Grid. However, revenue of these projects declined by 34% to around PKR 9.7 billion, compared to PKR 14.7 billion last year, mainly on account of settlement of the debt-related tariff component.

FPCL registered net profitability of PKR 4.5 billion during the year. Pursuant to the regulatory and shareholders' approval, FFC's stake in FPCL increased to full control effective January 2026. 16 million shares of FFC have been issued to Fauji Foundation (FF) in exchange of 215 million shares of FPCL acquired from FF.

Agritech Limited (AGL) remains strategically important for the Group. During the year, FFC increased its investment in AGL through an additional investment of PKR 5.18 billion, including acquisition of equity shares and other debt instruments, resulting in aggregate equity stake increasing to 37.36% at year end. Agritech Limited reported net profit of PKR 4.4 billion for the year. The enhanced shareholding supports the Group's objective of ensuring reliable supply of urea and food security in the country.

AKBL attained a profit after tax of PKR 24.7 billion during the reporting period, and contributed the highest share of profit of PKR 16 billion among the Group's associates. The Bank's performance was driven by continued focus on low-cost deposits and expansion in the retail segment.
